modules.title: Hyperkalaemia: don't miss the ECG, don't under-dose the calcium

bullets.text: Severe hyperkalaemia is usually defined as K+ 6.5 mmol/L or above
ECG progression: peaked T waves, then broad QRS, then sine wave, then arrest
A normal ECG does not exclude it — sensitivity is poor
Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV to stabilise the myocardium. Repeat if no ECG change
Insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g IV. Monitor glucose for at least 6 hours
Then treat the cause and consider potassium removal. Discuss with renal early

deep_dive.heading: Sequence at the bedside
steps: Attach continuous cardiac monitoring before anything else
12-lead ECG and repeat venous gas to confirm — rule out a haemolysed sample
Calcium first if there are ECG changes: it buys time but does not lower K+
Insulin-dextrose next: onset roughly 15 minutes, peak effect at about 1 hour
Salbutamol nebulisers are an adjunct only, never a substitute
Ask why: AKI, drugs (ACEi, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim), rhabdomyolysis, Addison's

quiz.question: A 72-year-old on ramipril and spironolactone is weak. K+ 7.1 mmol/L, ECG shows a broad QRS. Which drug goes in first?
options: Insulin 10 units IV
Calcium gluconate IV
Salbutamol 10 mg nebulised
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV
quiz.explanation: Calcium stabilises the myocardium and is the first drug when there are ECG changes. It does not lower K+ — follow it immediately with insulin and dextrose.

source.title: Treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults

modules.title: Occlusion MI: the patterns that don't meet STEMI criteria

bullets.text: Millimetre STEMI criteria miss a substantial minority of acute occlusions
Posterior MI: horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves
Do posterior leads V7 to V9 — only 0.5 mm elevation is needed there
De Winter pattern: upsloping ST depression with tall symmetrical T waves
Modified Sgarbossa criteria apply when there is LBBB or a paced rhythm
Ongoing pain with a dynamic ECG warrants a cardiology conversation, not a wait

deep_dive.heading: What to do with the suspicion
points: Repeat the ECG every 10 to 15 minutes while pain continues
Compare with any previous ECG before calling a change new
Record posterior and right-sided leads and label them clearly on the trace
Escalate on the pattern and the story, not on whether the millimetres are met

quiz.question: Chest pain, ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. Next step?
options: Treat as NSTEMI and admit
Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Give thrombolysis
Repeat troponin at 3 hours and reassess
quiz.explanation: This is the mirror image of posterior injury. Posterior leads confirm it, and only 0.5 mm of elevation in V7 to V9 is required.

source.title: ECG library — posterior myocardial infarction

modules.title: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline early, and what to do when it doesn't work

bullets.text: Adult dose: adrenaline 500 micrograms IM into the anterolateral thigh
Repeat every 5 minutes if there is no improvement
Refractory means no improvement after two appropriate IM doses
Refractory anaphylaxis needs an adrenaline infusion and expert help
Lay the patient flat — sitting or standing up has been linked to arrest
Steroids are no longer routinely recommended in the initial treatment

deep_dive.heading: If two IM doses have not worked
steps: Call for senior and critical care help now
Start an adrenaline infusion per your local protocol and stop repeat IM dosing
Give a rapid IV fluid bolus — distributive shock is often profound
Consider whether this is airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention
Observe after recovery: biphasic reactions occur, so follow local observation periods
Serial mast cell tryptase, adrenaline autoinjector, and an allergy referral before discharge

quiz.question: An adult with anaphylaxis has had two doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart with no improvement. What is the next step?
options: A third IM dose
IV adrenaline bolus 1 mg
Start an adrenaline infusion and call for critical care help
Give hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
quiz.explanation: This is refractory anaphylaxis. Guidance moves to an adrenaline infusion with expert help rather than continued repeat IM dosing.

source.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers

modules.title: Adult DKA: the four things that go wrong in the first two hours

bullets.text: Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour — weight-based, not a standard rate
Continue long-acting basal insulin. Stopping it causes rebound ketosis
Add glucose-containing fluid once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L
Potassium falls fast — check it early and replace within the infusion
Resolution is ketone and pH based, not glucose based
Euglycaemic DKA happens on SGLT2 inhibitors — check ketones despite normal glucose

deep_dive.heading: Traps worth naming at handover
points: Do not withhold potassium replacement waiting for a formal lab result if the gas shows it
Bicarbonate is not routine and can worsen intracellular acidosis
A rising glucose on treatment usually means the infusion is not actually running
Look for the precipitant: infection, missed insulin, MI, pregnancy, drugs

quiz.question: A patient in DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor has a blood glucose of 9 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: DKA is excluded by the normal glucose
Euglycaemic DKA is recognised and ketones must be checked
Insulin should be withheld until glucose exceeds 14 mmol/L
Only sodium bicarbonate will correct the acidosis
quiz.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. Diagnosis rests on ketones and acidosis, and treatment runs with glucose-containing fluid alongside insulin.

source.title: The management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults
source.publisher: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care

modules.title: Paediatric shock: 10 mL/kg, then reassess

bullets.text: Bolus 10 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid, then reassess before the next one
Reassess after every bolus: heart rate, perfusion, conscious level, liver edge
Look for crackles, a new gallop or an enlarging liver — signs of fluid overload
In DKA and severe malnutrition the approach is different — follow those pathways
If shock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, think inotropes and critical care, not more fluid
Weight: use the child's actual weight if known, otherwise an age-based formula

deep_dive.heading: Why the volume changed
points: Practice moved away from routine 20 mL/kg boluses towards smaller volumes with reassessment
The concern is fluid overload and delayed recognition of the child who needs vasoactive support
The reassessment matters more than the number — a bolus given without review is the real error
Get the vasoactive drug conversation started early rather than after the fourth bolus

quiz.question: A 4-year-old with septic shock remains tachycardic and poorly perfused after 40 mL/kg of crystalloid. What is the priority?
options: Another 20 mL/kg bolus
Start vasoactive support and involve critical care
Wait for the lactate to return
Change to colloid
quiz.explanation: Persisting shock after substantial fluid should prompt vasoactive support and critical care involvement rather than continued escalating boluses.

source.title: Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management (NG51)

modules.title: Fever under 3 months: the ones you do not send home

bullets.text: Under 3 months with fever 38°C or above is a red flag in its own right
Serious bacterial infection can present with no localising signs at all
The traffic light system does not apply below 3 months in the usual way
Hypothermia in a neonate is as concerning as fever
A well-looking baby who fed poorly overnight still needs a senior review
Document the parental concern — it is a recognised risk marker

deep_dive.heading: At the whiteboard
points: Ask what has changed at home: feeding, wet nappies, tone, colour, cry
Check the observations against age-specific ranges, not adult intuition
Follow the local neonatal sepsis pathway for investigations and antibiotic timing
If you are discharging any infant under 3 months, that decision is a senior one

quiz.question: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.2°C, is feeding normally and looks well. What is the correct approach?
options: Discharge with safety-net advice
Follow the under-3-month febrile infant pathway with senior involvement
Oral antibiotics and GP review
Reassure — the traffic light system says green
quiz.explanation: Age under 3 months with fever is a high-risk feature regardless of appearance. Local febrile infant pathways and senior review apply.

source.title: Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (NG143)

modules.title: Aortic dissection: the presentations that look like something else

bullets.text: Pain is often abrupt and maximal at onset rather than crescendo
Beware the stroke, limb ischaemia or syncope with chest or back pain
A normal chest X-ray and a normal D-dimer do not exclude it
Inferior ST elevation can be dissection involving the right coronary ostium
Ask about pulse and blood pressure differences, but their absence proves nothing
If you are seriously considering it, the test is a CT aortogram

deep_dive.heading: The trap worth naming
points: Anticoagulating a dissection as an ACS is the classic catastrophic error
Malperfusion syndromes explain the odd neurological or abdominal presentation
Control heart rate and blood pressure once suspected, and discuss with vascular or cardiothoracics early
Document explicitly why you did or did not image — it is a common complaint theme

quiz.question: A 58-year-old has sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back and a new right hemiparesis. BP differs by 30 mmHg between arms. What is the priority investigation?
options: CT head only
CT aortogram
D-dimer
Bedside echocardiogram alone
quiz.explanation: Sudden chest and back pain with neurological deficit suggests dissection with carotid malperfusion. CT aortogram is the diagnostic test, and thrombolysis would be dangerous.

source.title: RCEMLearning — aortic dissection

modules.title: Thunderclap headache: what the 6-hour CT does and does not do

bullets.text: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset has very high sensitivity for SAH
That performance depends on a modern scanner and a competent reporter
Beyond 6 hours, sensitivity falls and further investigation is needed
LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset to allow xanthochromia to form
Send CSF for spectrophotometry, and protect the sample from light
Onset time is the anchor for everything — pin it down precisely

deep_dive.heading: The conversation with the patient
points: Explain the residual risk if they decline the LP, and document that discussion
CT angiography is an alternative pathway in some units — know what yours does
A traumatic tap is not a reason to stop thinking; red cell counts alone are unreliable
Consider the alternatives: dissection, venous sinus thrombosis, reversible vasoconstriction

quiz.question: A patient presents 9 hours after a thunderclap headache. Non-contrast CT head is normal. What is appropriate?
options: Discharge — a normal CT excludes SAH
Immediate LP now
Plan LP at 12 hours or more from headache onset, or an agreed local alternative pathway
Repeat CT at 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Beyond 6 hours a normal CT does not exclude SAH. LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset so xanthochromia can be detected, unless your unit uses a CTA-based pathway.

source.title: RCEMLearning — subarachnoid haemorrhage

modules.title: Paracetamol overdose: the questions that change management

bullets.text: Single time of ingestion, or staggered over more than an hour? It changes everything
The UK uses a single treatment line on the nomogram at 4 hours post-ingestion
Levels before 4 hours cannot be interpreted on the nomogram
Staggered and unknown-time overdoses are treated without waiting for a level
Check TOXBASE for the current regimen — it has changed more than once
Do not stop acetylcysteine for a rash alone; treat and continue

deep_dive.heading: Before the patient leaves
points: End-of-treatment bloods matter: ALT, INR, creatinine and a paracetamol level
Rising ALT or INR means continuing treatment and a liver unit conversation
Every overdose gets a mental health assessment and a capacity-aware risk discussion
Ask about co-ingestants, and about what the patient expected to happen

quiz.question: A patient took paracetamol in unknown amounts over about 8 hours. What is the correct approach?
options: Wait for a 4-hour level
Treat as a staggered overdose without waiting for a level, per TOXBASE
Plot the level on the nomogram from the first tablet
Discharge if asymptomatic
quiz.explanation: The nomogram only applies to a single ingestion at a known time. Staggered overdoses are managed on the TOXBASE pathway without relying on a plotted level.

source.title: TOXBASE (NPIS) — paracetamol

modules.title: Head injury: the anticoagulated patient and the 'minor' bang

bullets.text: Anticoagulation changes the threshold for imaging even without other risk factors
Ask what they are on: DOAC, warfarin, antiplatelet — they are not equivalent
Falls in older people are frequently under-triaged as minor
Reduced GCS with no history is a head injury until proven otherwise
Know your reversal pathway and where the agents are kept before you need them
Discharge advice must be given to someone who will actually be with the patient

deep_dive.heading: Things that get missed
points: The mechanism was not trivial if the patient could not protect themselves on the way down
Consider why they fell — syncope, arrhythmia, sepsis, medication
Chronic subdural presents as confusion or unsteadiness weeks later, not as a headache
Check the C-spine properly in the older patient; injuries there are commonly missed

quiz.question: An 82-year-old on apixaban had an unwitnessed fall, hit her head, and is fully alert with no focal deficit. What is the appropriate action?
options: Discharge with head injury advice
CT head in line with the anticoagulated head injury pathway
Observe for 4 hours then discharge
Skull X-ray
quiz.explanation: Anticoagulation lowers the imaging threshold in head injury. A normal GCS does not exclude significant intracranial bleeding in this group.

source.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

modules.title: Testicular torsion: the clock started before they arrived

bullets.text: Acute scrotal pain in a young male is torsion until surgically excluded
Salvage rates fall steeply with time from onset of pain
Abdominal or groin pain with no scrotal complaint still needs the testes examined
Ultrasound must never delay a surgical opinion
Intermittent pain that has settled is still a torsion story
Document the examination, including that you examined at all

deep_dive.heading: Why this keeps appearing in claims
points: Pain referred to the abdomen leads to the genitalia never being examined
A normal-looking scrotum early on gives false reassurance
Waiting for a scan out of hours is a recurring cause of delay
Adolescents may not volunteer the symptom — ask directly and offer a chaperone

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has 3 hours of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. What must be part of the assessment?
options: Urine dip only
Examination of the testes
Abdominal X-ray
Discharge with a surgical review in the morning
quiz.explanation: Torsion frequently presents as abdominal pain. Failure to examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain is a well-documented cause of delayed diagnosis.

source.title: RCEMLearning — testicular torsion

modules.title: Preoxygenation: the three minutes that decide how the RSI goes

bullets.text: Sit the patient up unless there is a specific reason not to
A well-sealed mask matters more than the flow rate on the flowmeter
Nasal cannulae left on during laryngoscopy extend safe apnoea time
The shocked and acidotic patient desaturates fast — plan for it, don't be surprised
Say the plan aloud: who does what, and what happens if the first look fails
Have push-dose vasopressor drawn up before induction, not after

deep_dive.heading: The 60 seconds before you push drugs
steps: Position: ear to sternal notch, head up
Preoxygenate with a tight seal and add nasal oxygen underneath
Optimise haemodynamics first — fluid or vasopressor before induction
State the plan A, B, C out loud and name who does each
Confirm suction is working and within reach of the intubator
Confirm the failed-airway equipment is open and the person who will use it knows

quiz.question: Which intervention most reliably prolongs safe apnoea time during laryngoscopy?
options: Increasing the tidal volume of bag-mask breaths
Leaving nasal cannula oxygen running through the apnoeic period
Using a smaller tube
Reducing the induction agent dose
quiz.explanation: Apnoeic oxygenation via nasal cannulae maintained through laryngoscopy extends the time to desaturation, particularly in patients with limited reserve.

source.title: Guidelines for the management of tracheal intubation in critically ill adults
source.publisher: Difficult Airway Society / FICM / ICS / RCoA

modules.title: RSI — The Pre-Induction Checklist That Prevents Peri-Intubation Arrest

bullets.text: Pre-oxygenate to SpO2 >94% — sit upright, tight mask seal, 15 L/min O2 for ≥3 minutes or 8 vital-capacity breaths
Apnoeic oxygenation: 15 L/min via nasal cannulae left running throughout laryngoscopy extends safe apnoea time significantly
DASH-1A checklist: MAP ≥65 mmHg, Haemoglobin adequate, Glucose 4–10 mmol/L — correct all three before pushing drugs
Induction agent: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV for haemodynamic instability; propofol 1–2 mg/kg where haemodynamics are stable
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg IV is the standard paralytic; suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg if rapid offset required (contraindicated in hyperkalaemia, burns >24h, denervation)
Failed intubation drill (DAS 2015): declare failed after 3 attempts, maintain oxygenation as the priority, call for surgical airway early
Post-intubation: sedate + paralyse for transfer, target SpO2 94–98%, PaCO2 4.5–6 kPa, ventilate 6–8 mL/kg IBW

deep_dive.heading: DAS 2015 Failed Intubation Pathway
steps: Plan A: direct or video laryngoscopy — maximum 3 attempts by experienced operator
Maintain oxygenation between each attempt; use IGEL or LMA if mask ventilation fails
Plan B: supraglottic airway device (SGA) — declare cant-intubate-can-oxygenate and call for help
Plan C: wake the patient if SGA provides adequate oxygenation and intubation not immediately essential
Plan D: cant-intubate-cant-oxygenate (CICO) — front-of-neck airway (FONA) with scalpel-bougie-tube technique immediately
After any difficult airway: document in notes, alert the patient, complete Difficult Airway Alert Form

quiz.question: A 78-year-old in respiratory failure requires intubation. BP 78/50 mmHg. Which induction agent is most appropriate?
options: Propofol 2 mg/kg
Thiopentone 5 mg/kg
Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg
Midazolam 0.3 mg/kg without a paralytic
quiz.explanation: Ketamine maintains sympathetic tone and is haemodynamically safer in shocked patients. Propofol causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, worsening hypotension. Thiopentone similarly reduces SVR. Midazolam alone without a paralytic is not RSI.

source.title: Difficult Airway Society Guidelines for Unanticipated Difficult Intubation

modules.title: High-Sensitivity Troponin — Reading the Numbers Correctly

bullets.text: hs-cTnI and hs-cTnT are different assays with different reference limits — always check your local lab's 99th-percentile upper reference limit (URL)
ESC 0h/1h algorithm: if 0h value <5 ng/L AND absolute rise <3 ng/L at 1h, rule-out sensitivity exceeds 99%
Significant delta: a rise ≥3–5 ng/L (absolute) between 0h and 1h samples is considered significant — relative percentage rise alone is unreliable
Non-ACS causes of troponin elevation: PE, myocarditis, demand ischaemia, renal failure, sepsis, stroke, tachyarrhythmia — do not equate elevation with ACS
HEART score ≤3 with low-risk delta: suitable for early discharge pathway; HEART ≥7 warrants same-day cardiology review
LEGEND trial: hs-cTnI limit-of-detection strategy (LoD <1.6 ng/L) allows safe 0h rule-out for low-prevalence populations in the ED
Always pair troponin with a structured pre-test probability score — troponin without clinical context is diagnostically dangerous

deep_dive.heading: When a Positive Troponin Is Not ACS
points: Type 2 MI (demand ischaemia): tachyarrhythmia, sepsis, anaemia — troponin rises but coronaries may be normal; treat the underlying cause
Myocarditis: young patient, viral prodrome, pleuritic chest pain, ECG changes across multiple territories — MRI, not angiogram
PE: RV strain pattern on ECG, elevated D-dimer, Wells score — troponin predicts RV dysfunction not coronary disease
The delta is key: a single elevated troponin without dynamic rise over time usually means chronic elevation, not acute occlusion
Document pre-test probability explicitly — this drives the downstream investigation plan

quiz.question: A 55-year-old with atypical chest pain has hs-cTnI 6 ng/L at 0h and 7 ng/L at 1h (local URL 52 ng/L). Which statement is correct?
options: ACS is confirmed — activate the cath lab
Both values are below the URL and the delta is <3 ng/L — this meets low-risk ESC 0h/1h rule-out criteria
A third troponin at 3h is mandatory before any decision
The patient must be admitted to the coronary care unit
quiz.explanation: Both values are well below the 99th-percentile URL and the absolute delta of 1 ng/L is below the 3 ng/L threshold. This meets ESC 0h/1h rule-out criteria if clinical assessment is concordant — early discharge with HEART score stratification is appropriate.

source.title: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes

modules.title: DKA in the ED — Fluids, Insulin, Potassium in the Right Order

bullets.text: Diagnosis: ketonaemia ≥3 mmol/L (or ketonuria 2+), blood glucose >11 mmol/L (or known T1DM), venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L
Fluid: 0.9% NaCl 1 L in first hour; SCOPE-1 RCT suggests Hartmann's (balanced crystalloid) may reduce acidosis duration — check local protocol
Fixed-rate insulin infusion (FRII): 0.1 units/kg/h — do NOT start if K+ <3.5 mmol/L; continue long-acting basal insulin throughout treatment
Potassium: add 40 mmol/L KCl to fluids once K+ <5.5 mmol/L and urine output confirmed; target K+ 4–5 mmol/L
Add glucose 10% alongside insulin when blood glucose <14 mmol/L to prevent hypoglycaemia while continuing ketone clearance
Resolution criteria (JBDS): ketones <0.3 mmol/L, venous pH >7.3, bicarbonate >18 mmol/L — NOT simply when glucose normalises
Euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors: glucose may be near-normal — check ketones in all sick diabetics regardless of glucose level

deep_dive.heading: JBDS DKA Hourly Monitoring Targets
steps: 0h: confirm diagnosis, IV access, fluid resuscitation 0.9% NaCl 1 L/h, baseline bloods including VBG and ketones
1h: if K+ ≥3.5 mmol/L, start FRII 0.1 units/kg/h
Target: ketones falling ≥0.5 mmol/L/h OR bicarbonate rising ≥3 mmol/L/h OR glucose falling ≥3 mmol/L/h
If targets not met at 1h: increase FRII by 1 unit/h (not by increasing fluid rate arbitrarily)
Add 10% glucose once BG <14 mmol/L — do NOT reduce insulin at this point
Cerebral oedema risk: headache or altered GCS during treatment → immediate critical care involvement

quiz.question: A 24-year-old type 1 diabetic has pH 7.20, ketones 4.5 mmol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, K+ 3.2 mmol/L. Which action is most important before starting insulin?
options: Give sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV
Start FRII immediately at 0.1 units/kg/h
Replace potassium first — do not start insulin with K+ <3.5 mmol/L
Give a 2 L bolus of 0.9% NaCl before any insulin
quiz.explanation: Insulin drives K+ intracellularly, worsening hypokalaemia. Starting FRII with K+ <3.5 mmol/L risks fatal arrhythmia. Correct potassium to ≥3.5 mmol/L first, then initiate insulin. Bicarbonate is not routinely indicated and can worsen intracellular acidosis.

source.title: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults (3rd edition)
source.publisher: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care

modules.title: Shock — Four Types, One Bedside Framework

bullets.text: Distributive: high CO, low SVR — warm peripheries, bounding pulse; vasopressor choice: noradrenaline 0.01–3 mcg/kg/min; add vasopressin for refractory septic shock
Cardiogenic: low CO, high SVR — cool clammy peripheries, raised JVP; avoid aggressive fluids; LV vs RV failure requires fundamentally different management
Obstructive: PE (JVP raised, RV strain ECG), tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation), tamponade (Beck's triad) — treat the cause urgently
Hypovolaemic: low CO, high SVR — look for source; haemorrhage requires early blood products not just crystalloid
RUSH protocol (Rapid Ultrasound for Shock and Hypotension): assess heart, IVC, aorta, pleural/pericardial spaces — differentiates shock type within minutes
RV failure management: avoid tachycardia, maintain RV preload, avoid vasodilators, consider adrenaline infusion rather than noradrenaline
If MAP remains <65 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor is indicated regardless of aetiology

deep_dive.heading: RUSH Protocol — Rapid Ultrasound for Shock
steps: Pump: subxiphoid view — assess LV function, RV size, pericardial effusion
Tank (preload): IVC diameter and collapsibility — >2 cm non-collapsing suggests fluid overload; <1 cm with >50% collapse suggests hypovolaemia
Tank (fluid in wrong place): bilateral pleural effusions, ascites
Pipes: aortic aneurysm — measure at three levels; exclude AAA in all undifferentiated shock
Lung windows: B-lines (pulmonary oedema), absence of sliding (pneumothorax)
Synthesise: combine findings to classify shock type and guide immediate management

quiz.question: A 68-year-old is hypotensive with raised JVP, muffled heart sounds, and pulsus paradoxus. POCUS shows a pericardial effusion with RV diastolic collapse. Which treatment is immediately indicated?
options: Urgent pericardiocentesis
Noradrenaline infusion
IV furosemide 40 mg
1 L crystalloid bolus and reassess
quiz.explanation: This is cardiac tamponade with haemodynamic compromise — obstructive shock. Pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment. Fluids are a short-term temporising bridge only. Vasodilators and diuretics are contraindicated.

source.title: RUSH Exam — Rapid Ultrasound in Shock

modules.title: Tranexamic Acid — The Evidence Base and Its Limits

bullets.text: Mechanism: antifibrinolytic — inhibits plasminogen activation and plasmin, preserving formed clot; TXA is NOT procoagulant
CRASH-2 (20,211 patients): TXA 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8h reduced all-cause mortality; RR 0.91 (ARR ~1.5% in first 3h group)
Time window is critical: give within 3 hours of injury — mortality reduction disappears and may increase if given after 3 hours
Major haemorrhage protocol: give TXA ASAP — aim within 1 hour; prehospital TXA now standard in UK PHEM/HEMS practice
WOMAN trial (postpartum haemorrhage): TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours of delivery reduced death from PPH (RR 0.81) — now recommended by NICE
Topical TXA for epistaxis: 500 mg in 5 mL soaked gauze — reduces rebleeding and procedure time in RCTs
CRASH-3 (SAH): TXA did not reduce disability or death overall; possible benefit within 3h but increased cerebral ischaemic events — not standard UK practice

deep_dive.heading: Why the Time Window Matters
points: Hyperfibrinolysis peaks in the first 1–3 hours after injury — TXA blocks this critical window
Late TXA (>3h) may paradoxically increase mortality — possibly by blocking late physiological fibrinolysis needed for clot resolution
CRASH-2 subgroup: greatest benefit in those with SBP <75 mmHg — the most shocked patients benefit most
Dose: 1 g IV loading dose over 10 min, then 1 g infusion over 8h — must not give as a rapid bolus (seizure risk)
TXA is cheap, widely available, and low-risk when given in time — the barrier to use should be low in major haemorrhage

quiz.question: A 32-year-old arrives 2.5 hours after a high-speed RTC with haemodynamic instability and suspected internal haemorrhage. Which statement regarding TXA is correct?
options: TXA is contraindicated in blunt trauma
TXA 1 g IV should be given now — within the 3-hour window
TXA is only indicated if fibrinogen is confirmed low on TEG
TXA should be withheld until haemostatic surgery is confirmed
quiz.explanation: CRASH-2 evidence supports giving TXA as early as possible in major trauma haemorrhage, with benefit up to 3 hours from injury. Waiting for lab confirmation delays treatment and misses the time-dependent window. Dose: 1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8h.

source.title: CRASH-2 trial — tranexamic acid in trauma

modules.title: Paediatric Resuscitation — Doses, Rhythms, and Why Children Are Different

bullets.text: Weight estimation: (age + 4) × 2 kg for 1–10 years (APLS formula); Broselow tape for rapid bedside use; PAWPER tape reduces error in obese children
Defibrillation: 4 J/kg for ALL DC shocks — first, second, and subsequent; the 2+4+4 J/kg sequence is historical — current RCUK 2021 recommends 4 J/kg throughout
Adrenaline: 10 mcg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000) every 3–5 minutes in arrest — same intervals as adults
Amiodarone: 5 mg/kg IV/IO for shock-refractory VF/pVT — given after 3rd shock, repeated after 5th shock
Non-shockable rhythms (PEA/asystole) predominate in paediatric arrest because cause is usually hypoxic — CPR quality and rapid airway management are the priorities
Paediatric airway differences: large occiput causes neck flexion, large tongue, anterior larynx, narrowest point at cricoid — uncuffed tubes to age 8 acceptable but cuffed preferred
Post-arrest: ThAALO RCT showed targeted temperature management (32–34°C vs 36°C) did not improve survival; fever MUST be avoided regardless

deep_dive.heading: Paediatric ALS Sequence (RCUK 2021)
steps: Unresponsive, not breathing normally: call for help, start CPR 15:2 (two-rescuer) — 30:2 if alone
Rhythm check every 2 minutes: VF/pVT → defibrillate 4 J/kg; PEA/asystole → continue CPR
IO access if IV fails after 60 seconds in arrest — tibial tuberosity or humeral head
Adrenaline 10 mcg/kg every 3–5 min: non-shockable rhythm from start; shockable rhythm after 3rd shock
Address 4Hs and 4Ts: hypoxia is the most common paediatric cause — early high-quality airway management
ROSC: avoid hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, hyperthermia — 4-hourly glucose checks for 24h post-arrest

quiz.question: A 6-year-old (20 kg) is in VF arrest. CPR is underway. What is the correct defibrillation energy for the first shock?
quiz.explanation: Current RCUK guidelines (2021) recommend 4 J/kg for all shocks in paediatric VF/pVT. For a 20 kg child: 4 × 20 = 80 J. The older 2+4+4 J/kg sequence is no longer recommended.

source.title: Paediatric Advanced Life Support Guidelines 2021

modules.title: Stroke — The Time-Critical Pathway From Door to Decision

bullets.text: BE-FAST (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time) has higher sensitivity than FAST alone — posterior circulation strokes are commonly missed by FAST
Stroke mimics: hypoglycaemia (check BM first), Todd's paresis post-seizure, hemiplegic migraine — BM must be checked before any stroke alert is activated
Thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg): time window 0–4.5 hours from onset; contraindications include SBP >185, glucose <2.8 or >22, platelets <100, therapeutic anticoagulation
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) is now used in many UK centres as a single-bolus alternative — EXTEND-IA TNK shows non-inferiority to alteplase
LVO detection pre-alert tools: FAST-ED (score ≥4) and RACE (score ≥5) predict large vessel occlusion with sensitivity ~70–80% — use to pre-alert thrombectomy centre
BP before thrombolysis: treat if SBP >185/110 — labetalol 10–20 mg IV or GTN infusion; target ≤185/110 to allow thrombolysis
Do NOT treat hypertension if thrombolysis is NOT being given — unless >220/120; permissive hypertension aids penumbra perfusion

deep_dive.heading: Stroke Pathway — Time Targets
steps: Door to CT: ≤25 minutes — non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage
Door to needle (thrombolysis): ≤60 minutes — SSNAP/RCP national audit target
Simultaneously: BM, 12-lead ECG (AF detection), bloods, IV access × 2, NIHSS score
CT angiography for all eligible patients: identifies LVO for EVT referral — do not delay thrombolysis for CTA
Door to groin puncture (EVT): ≤90 minutes at thrombectomy-capable centre
Pre-alert Stroke team and neurovascular centre before patient arrives — time is brain = 1.9 million neurons/min

quiz.question: A 62-year-old has sudden left arm weakness and dysarthria, onset 90 minutes ago. BM 6.2 mmol/L, BP 190/100, CT head normal. Which is the most appropriate next action?
options: Observe for 4 hours and reassess
Give IV alteplase after treating BP to ≤185/110
Withhold thrombolysis — BP is a contraindication
Give aspirin 300 mg immediately and refer to TIA clinic
quiz.explanation: BP of 190/100 is above the thrombolysis threshold but can be treated with labetalol or GTN to ≤185/110. BP alone is not a permanent contraindication. This presentation is within the 4.5h window and warrants thrombolysis once BP is controlled.

modules.title: Brugada Syndrome — The Three Patterns and Sudden Death Risk

bullets.text: Type 1 (diagnostic): coved ST elevation ≥2 mm in V1–V2 with negative T-wave — this is the ONLY spontaneously diagnostic pattern
Type 2 (saddleback): ≥2 mm high takeoff, convex ST elevation followed by positive T — requires drug challenge to confirm; NOT diagnostic alone
High right precordial leads: record V1–V2 at 2nd and 3rd ICS (high-leads position) — converts Type 2 to Type 1 in up to 30% of cases
Fever unmasks Brugada — any febrile young male with Type 1 pattern needs aggressive antipyretics and urgent cardiology review
SCN5A mutation (sodium channel gene): autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; male:female ratio 8:1; peak age 40s; Asian males overrepresented
Avoid sodium channel blockers (flecainide, procainamide, ajmaline, propafenone) — they precipitate VF in Brugada patients
ED management: treat fever aggressively (paracetamol 1 g IV), avoid precipitating drugs, call cardiology, ICD referral for symptomatic patients

deep_dive.heading: Drugs That Unmask or Provoke Brugada Pattern
points: Class Ia sodium channel blockers: ajmaline, procainamide — used diagnostically to unmask Type 2 to Type 1 (only in supervised cardiology setting)
Class 1c agents: flecainide, propafenone — DANGEROUS in established Brugada; never give in ED
Tricyclic antidepressants, lithium, cocaine — can provoke VF in Brugada carriers
Non-cardiac drugs of concern: carbamazepine, phenytoin, high-dose propofol — document Brugada diagnosis prominently
Differentials for Type 1 pattern: early repolarisation, RBBB, pericarditis, myocarditis, hypothermia, hyperkalaemia — clinical context is essential

quiz.question: A 38-year-old Asian male presents with fever (38.9°C) and palpitations. ECG shows coved ST elevation ≥2 mm in V1 with negative T-wave. What is the most important immediate action?
options: Give flecainide 150 mg orally for rate control
Arrange urgent ECG stress test
Treat fever aggressively with paracetamol and seek urgent cardiology review
Discharge with 24-hour Holter monitor
quiz.explanation: This is a fever-unmasked Type 1 Brugada pattern — genuinely diagnostic. Fever can trigger VF in Brugada syndrome; aggressive antipyretics and urgent cardiology input are the priorities. Flecainide is absolutely contraindicated as a sodium channel blocker.

modules.title: WPW and Pre-Excitation — The Delta Wave and Why Pre-Excited AF Kills

bullets.text: WPW triad: short PR (<120 ms), slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), widened QRS (>120 ms) — due to accessory pathway bypassing AV node
AVRT (orthodromic): narrow complex regular tachycardia — conduction antegrade through AV node, retrograde via accessory pathway; adenosine is safe in this situation
Pre-excited AF: broad, irregular, fast (>200 bpm) with varying QRS morphology — accessory pathway conducts AF without AV nodal filtering; risk of degeneration to VF
NEVER give AV-nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited AF: adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers — all enhance accessory pathway conduction and may precipitate VF
Treatment of pre-excited AF: DC cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable; procainamide IV (15 mg/kg over 30 min) or flecainide if stable — slows accessory pathway conduction
Rate >200 bpm in a broad, irregular tachycardia strongly suggests accessory pathway conduction — the AV node cannot conduct at this rate
Long-term: electrophysiology study (EPS) and radiofrequency ablation curative in >95% of cases; refer all symptomatic WPW to cardiology

deep_dive.heading: How to Tell Pre-Excited AF From VT
points: Pre-excited AF: broad AND irregular with varying QRS morphology — VT is usually regular
Rate >200 bpm suggests accessory pathway — AV node cannot conduct at this speed
Look for delta waves in sinus rhythm leads on the same ECG if available
When in doubt: assume VT and cardiovert — it is always safer to over-treat than to give AV-nodal blockers
After cardioversion: 12-lead in sinus rhythm to confirm WPW, then cardiology EPS referral

quiz.question: A 25-year-old has palpitations. HR 240 bpm, BP 100/70. ECG shows a broad, fast, irregular tachycardia with varying QRS morphology. Which drug is CONTRAINDICATED?
options: Procainamide
DC cardioversion
Adenosine
Flecainide
quiz.explanation: This is pre-excited AF. Adenosine (and verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) block the AV node but preferentially enhance accessory pathway conduction, potentially precipitating VF. DC cardioversion or procainamide are appropriate. Flecainide slows the accessory pathway and is an alternative in stable patients.

modules.title: STEMI Equivalents — The ECGs That Activate the Cath Lab Without Classic Criteria

bullets.text: De Winter pattern: upsloping ST depression ≥1 mm at J-point in V1–V6 with tall, peaked symmetrical T-waves — represents proximal LAD occlusion; NO ST elevation present
Posterior STEMI: horizontal ST depression V1–V3 with dominant R waves (R>S in V2) — mirror image; confirm with posterior leads V7–V9 (≥0.5 mm elevation diagnostic)
Wellens syndrome Type A: biphasic T-waves V2–V3; Type B: deeply inverted symmetric T-waves V2–V3 — both indicate critical LAD proximal stenosis; do NOT exercise test

Modified Sgarbossa criteria for LBBB: concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm (score 5), concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3 (score 3), excessive discordant elevation >25% of S-wave (score 2); score ≥3 = STEMI equivalent
aVR ST elevation ≥1 mm with diffuse ST depression: suggests left main or proximal LAD occlusion — high mortality, needs emergent cath lab activation
Right ventricular MI: inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R — give IV fluids NOT nitrates; nitrates cause catastrophic BP drop in RV failure
Hyperacute T-waves: tall, broad-based, asymmetric T-waves in early STEMI — often transient and missed; compare with previous ECG if available

deep_dive.heading: Practical Actions When You See These Patterns
points: De Winter, posterior STEMI, aVR elevation: activate cath lab pathway as for STEMI — do not wait for troponin result
Wellens: patient is pain-free, ECG shows reperfusion injury — high re-occlusion risk; admit, avoid exercise testing, urgent cardiology review
Sgarbossa in LBBB: score ≥3 with ongoing chest pain warrants cath lab activation regardless of LBBB age
Right ventricular MI: right-sided leads V3R–V5R routine in all inferior STEMIs; treat shock with fluids and dobutamine, not vasodilators
Retrospective: if pain resolved and ECG normalised, serial ECGs and urgent cardiology outpatient review may be appropriate

quiz.question: A 55-year-old has crushing chest pain. ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with upright T-waves and dominant R wave in V2. Standard STEMI criteria are NOT met. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serial troponins and admit as NSTEMI
Record posterior leads V7–V9 and activate cath lab if ≥0.5 mm elevation confirmed
CT pulmonary angiogram to exclude PE
Discharge and arrange exercise tolerance test
quiz.explanation: This is posterior STEMI — anterior leads show the mirror image. Posterior leads V7–V9 confirm it with as little as 0.5 mm elevation. This is a STEMI equivalent requiring emergent cath lab activation. Serial troponins alone are insufficient.

modules.title: Broad Complex Tachycardia — Treat Everything as VT Until Proven Otherwise

bullets.text: Default rule: ALL broad complex tachycardias (QRS >120 ms, rate >100) are VT until proven otherwise — misdiagnosing VT as SVT-with-aberrancy and giving verapamil can cause cardiac arrest
Brugada 4-step algorithm: 1) RS complex absent in all precordials → VT; 2) RS interval >100 ms in any precordial → VT; 3) AV dissociation → VT; 4) VT morphology criteria met → VT
VT features: AV dissociation (independent P-waves), capture beats (narrow QRS), fusion beats (intermediate morphology), concordance (all precordials deflect same direction)
Polymorphic VT vs torsades de pointes: polymorphic VT needs urgent treatment of cause (ischaemia); TdP needs magnesium 2 g IV over 10 min, QT-prolonging drugs stopped, electrolyte correction
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR): broad complex rhythm 60–100 bpm during inferior STEMI reperfusion — benign; no treatment needed
Stable VT: amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min then 900 mg over 24h — do NOT give adenosine, verapamil, or beta-blockers
Unstable VT (haemodynamic compromise): synchronised DC cardioversion 200 J biphasic immediately — no time for drug loading

deep_dive.heading: Vereckei aVR Algorithm for Broad Complex Tachycardia
steps: Step 1: Is there an R wave in aVR? If yes → VT
Step 2: Is the width of initial R or Q in aVR >40 ms? If yes → VT
Step 3: Is there notching of the initial negative deflection in aVR? If yes → VT
Step 4: Is the vi/vt ratio ≤1? If yes → VT
If none of the above → SVT with aberrancy (rare to reach Step 4 in true VT)
Clinical principle: treat as VT regardless — the consequence of misdiagnosis is asymmetric

quiz.question: A 70-year-old with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy has a broad complex tachycardia at 160 bpm, BP 110/70. ECG shows concordant positive QRS complexes in all precordial leads. Which treatment is correct?
options: Adenosine 6 mg IV — to differentiate VT from SVT
Verapamil 5 mg IV — to slow the rate
Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes
Synchronised DC cardioversion 50 J immediately
quiz.explanation: This is VT (concordant precordials, history of IHD). The patient is haemodynamically stable, so pharmacological cardioversion with amiodarone is appropriate. Adenosine and verapamil can cause VF in VT. 200 J is correct if haemodynamically unstable — 50 J is insufficient.

modules.title: Paracetamol Overdose — NAPQI, the Nomogram, and When Liver Failure Follows

bullets.text: Mechanism: therapeutic doses undergo glucuronidation and sulphation; toxic doses generate NAPQI which accumulates as glutathione is depleted, causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis
UK nomogram: single treatment line at 100 mg/L at 4h, regardless of risk factors — superseded previous high-risk/normal-risk lines per MHRA 2012 guidance
Levels before 4h post-ingestion cannot be interpreted on the nomogram — wait or treat empirically if >150 mg/kg or >12 g ingested
Two-bag NAC regimen (2019 MHRA update): 100 mg/kg in 200 mL 5% glucose over 2h, then 200 mg/kg in 500 mL 5% glucose over 10h — reduces adverse reactions vs old three-bag
NAC anaphylactoid reaction: occurs in ~15%; slow infusion, give chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and hydrocortisone — do NOT stop NAC
Staggered overdose or unknown time: treat without waiting for level — nomogram does not apply; follow TOXBASE guidance
King's College Criteria for liver transplant referral: pH <7.3 after resuscitation OR (INR >6.5 + creatinine >300 μmol/L + grade III/IV encephalopathy)

deep_dive.heading: End-of-Treatment Assessment
points: Take bloods at end of NAC infusion: ALT, INR, creatinine, blood glucose, paracetamol level
Rising ALT or INR >2 at end of treatment: restart NAC and contact regional liver unit
Late presentation (>24h post-ingestion): high risk even with apparently subthreshold levels — discuss with NPIS/TOXBASE
Every overdose requires mental health assessment before discharge — this is a mandatory standard of care
Pregnancy: same treatment thresholds; consider obstetric review for fetal monitoring in significant overdoses

quiz.question: A patient took an unknown quantity of paracetamol over 4 hours throughout the evening. Level at 3h post-last-dose is 110 mg/L. What is correct?
options: Plot the level on the nomogram at 3h — below the line, no treatment
This is a staggered ingestion — the nomogram does not apply; treat with NAC per TOXBASE
Repeat the level at 4h and plot it then
Discharge as the level is <150 mg/L
quiz.explanation: A staggered ingestion over multiple hours cannot be plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, which only applies to a single ingestion at a known time. TOXBASE guidance is to treat with NAC regardless of level in staggered overdoses.

modules.title: Opioid Toxidrome — Naloxone Titration and the Duration Mismatch Problem

bullets.text: Classic triad: miosis (pinpoint pupils), CNS depression, respiratory depression — RR <12/min is the key life-threatening feature requiring naloxone
Naloxone IV: titrate 0.1–0.4 mg IV every 2–3 min; for arrest/apnoea: 0.8–2 mg IV/IM; intranasal 2 mg is effective if IV access is delayed
Duration mismatch is the key danger: naloxone half-life 45–90 min vs heroin 4–6h, methadone 24–72h — re-narcotisation after naloxone wears off is common and potentially fatal
Naloxone infusion: use if prolonged-acting opioid (methadone, slow-release preparations) — 2/3 of effective reversal dose per hour; monitor in resus for ≥12h

Partial reversal strategy: titrate naloxone to restore respiratory drive (RR >12/min) without precipitating full reversal — acute withdrawal causes agitation, pulmonary oedema, vomiting with aspiration risk
Novel opioids: illicit fentanyl analogues and nitazenes may require multiple mg of naloxone — do not assume standard dose is sufficient
Buprenorphine (high-affinity partial agonist): resistant to naloxone; higher doses (2–10 mg) required; ceiling effect on respiratory depression means respiratory arrest is less common

deep_dive.heading: Safe Discharge After Naloxone
steps: Short-acting opioid (heroin, codeine, tramadol): observe minimum 4–6 hours from last naloxone dose with maintained RR >12/min
Long-acting opioid (methadone, slow-release morphine): admit for minimum 12–24h monitoring with repeat doses or infusion
Unknown opioid or suspected synthetic fentanyl: treat as long-acting until proven otherwise
Re-narcotisation monitoring: GCS, RR, SpO2 documented every 30 min
Discharge criteria: RR consistently >12/min, GCS 15, SpO2 >94% on air, no further naloxone doses for ≥4h
Harm reduction at discharge: naloxone take-home prescription (ACCES scheme), community drug service referral

quiz.question: A 40-year-old on supervised methadone 80 mg/day is found unconscious. RR 4/min. Naloxone 0.8 mg IV given — consciousness returns. Thirty minutes later he becomes drowsy again. What is the correct action?
options: Discharge — he is now conscious and should be safe
Give another 0.8 mg IV and admit for naloxone infusion monitoring
Switch to intramuscular naloxone only
Naloxone is ineffective for methadone — intubate
quiz.explanation: Methadone has a half-life of 24–72 hours, far exceeding naloxone's 45–90 min. Re-narcotisation is expected and predicted. A naloxone infusion at 2/3 of the effective reversal dose per hour with minimum 12–24h monitoring is required. Naloxone DOES work for methadone.

modules.title: Stimulant Toxidrome — Cocaine, Amphetamines, and the Beta-Blocker Trap

bullets.text: Sympathomimetic toxidrome: tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, agitation — contrasts with opioid toxidrome (bradycardia, miosis, respiratory depression)
Cocaine sodium channel blockade: causes QRS widening, STEMI-like pattern, Brugada phenocopy — distinguish cocaine-related chest pain from true atherosclerotic STEMI
Cocaine chest pain: first-line benzodiazepines (diazepam 5–10 mg IV), GTN, aspirin, calcium channel blockers — NOT beta-blockers under any circumstances
Beta-blocker contraindication: blocks beta-adrenoceptors leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed → paradoxical hypertension and coronary vasospasm
MDMA hyponatraemia: SIADH mechanism with excess ADH release + water ingestion; particularly young females; Na+ can fall to <120 mmol/L → seizures, cerebral oedema
Hyperthermia management: target temperature <38.5°C with cooling mattress/ice packs; benzodiazepines IV; dantrolene 1–2.5 mg/kg IV if serotonin syndrome overlap
Rhabdomyolysis: CK >1000 U/L suggests muscle breakdown; IV fluids targeting urine output 200–300 mL/h; monitor K+ and renal function closely

deep_dive.heading: Cocaine Chest Pain — Is This ACS?
points: Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm AND thrombosis; true MI can occur in young patients with normal coronaries
ECG changes are common even without ischaemia — broad QRS suggests sodium channel toxicity, not necessarily occlusion
High-sensitivity troponin protocol still applies — up to 6% of cocaine chest pain patients have true MI
If STEMI confirmed with cocaine use: PCI preferred over thrombolysis (thrombotic mechanism often dominant)
Observation period: minimum 9–12h for cocaine chest pain with reassuring initial investigations

quiz.question: A 28-year-old who used cocaine has chest pain, HR 130, BP 190/110. ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in V1–V3. Which drug is CONTRAINDICATED?
options: Aspirin 300 mg
GTN sublingual
Metoprolol 5 mg IV
Lorazepam 2 mg IV
quiz.explanation: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in cocaine toxicity. Blocking beta-adrenergic vasodilation leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, worsening coronary vasospasm and hypertension. Benzodiazepines, GTN, and aspirin are appropriate first-line treatments.

source.title: Cocaine Toxicity — Emergency Management

modules.title: Serotonin Syndrome vs NMS — Hot, Rigid, and Confused: Which Is Which?

bullets.text: Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome (sensitivity 84%, specificity 97%): clonus (inducible/spontaneous/ocular) + one of: agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia, hypertonia — in context of serotonergic drug
Onset: serotonin syndrome is RAPID (within hours of drug addition); NMS is SLOW (days to weeks after antipsychotic exposure)
Key differentiator — clonus: the hallmark of serotonin syndrome; NOT present in NMS; examine lower limbs, ocular, and inducible clonus in every hot confused patient
NMS features: lead-pipe extrapyramidal rigidity (vs hyperreflexia in SS), hyperthermia, autonomic instability, reduced consciousness — caused by dopamine receptor blockade
Drug causes of SS: SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, triptans, fentanyl (weak), lithium, linezolid — ask about ALL medications including OTC
Treatment of SS: stop offending drug, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5–10 mg IV), cyproheptadine 12 mg orally (serotonin antagonist), cooling for hyperthermia
Treatment of NMS: stop antipsychotic, supportive ICU care, bromocriptine 2.5 mg TDS, dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV for severe hyperthermia — recovery days to weeks

deep_dive.heading: Other Hyperthermia Syndromes to Differentiate
points: Malignant hyperthermia: triggered by volatile anaesthetic agents or suxamethonium; genetic (RYR1 mutation); treatment is dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV — not the same as NMS
Anticholinergic syndrome: hot, dry, flushed, tachycardic, urinary retention, ileus, hallucinations — physostigmine in expert centres
Sympathomimetic toxidrome: wet (diaphoretic) vs anticholinergic (dry) — this distinction helps narrow the diagnosis
When in doubt: benzodiazepines are safe across all these syndromes — use while seeking toxicology advice
CK monitoring: all these syndromes can cause rhabdomyolysis — check CK, creatinine, urine output

quiz.question: A 35-year-old on citalopram and tramadol develops acute agitation, diaphoresis, and inducible clonus. Temperature 38.8°C. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Haloperidol 5 mg IV for acute agitation
Stop offending agents, benzodiazepines IV, cyproheptadine orally
Bromocriptine and dantrolene
Cooling blanket alone and observe
quiz.explanation: This meets Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome (clonus + agitation + diaphoresis on serotonergic agents). Immediate treatment: stop causative drugs, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist). Haloperidol could worsen outcome. Bromocriptine/dantrolene is for NMS.

source.title: Serotonin Syndrome — Hunter Criteria

modules.title: Beta-Blocker and CCB Overdose — High-Dose Insulin Is the Treatment, Not an Option

bullets.text: Presentation: bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, reduced consciousness — look-alikes are inferior MI, high spinal, hypothyroidism
CCB diagnostic clue: hyperglycaemia — calcium channel blockers inhibit insulin secretion from pancreatic beta-cells (vs beta-blockers → hypoglycaemia)
Immediate: atropine 500 mcg–3 mg IV (often fails in severe overdose), IV fluids, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose and ketone check
Calcium chloride 10%: 10 mL (1 g) IV over 5 min for CCB overdose — gives more ionised calcium than gluconate; repeat every 15–20 min for haemodynamic response
High-Dose Insulin Euglycaemic Therapy (HIET): 1 unit/kg IV bolus of actrapid then 1 unit/kg/h infusion — maintain BG 8–12 mmol/L, check glucose every 15–20 min
Lipid Emulsion Therapy (LET) 20%: 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 min then 0.25 mL/kg/min for 30–60 min — for refractory cardiac arrest from lipid-soluble agents
Escalation: VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock — early referral to ECMO-capable centre; do not wait for cardiac arrest before referring

deep_dive.heading: HIET — Practical Setup at the Bedside
steps: Prepare: 50% dextrose immediately available, glucometer on 15-min cycle, dedicated nursing resource
Bolus: actrapid 1 unit/kg IV (e.g., 70 units for 70 kg patient) — monitor closely for hypokalaemia
Infusion: 1 unit/kg/h — titrate to effect (target MAP ≥65, HR improvement)
Glucose supplementation: run 10% or 50% dextrose to maintain BG 8–12 mmol/L — glucose requirement varies widely
Potassium: check every 30–60 min; insulin drives K+ intracellularly — replace aggressively
Review at 30 min: if no haemodynamic improvement, escalate to lipid emulsion therapy and ECMO referral

quiz.question: A 60-year-old ingested 20 amlodipine tablets. HR 42, BP 65/40. ECG shows junctional bradycardia. Atropine 3 mg IV has had no effect. What is the most evidence-supported pharmacological intervention?
options: Digoxin 500 mcg IV
High-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy (1 unit/kg bolus then 1 unit/kg/h)
Adrenaline 1 mg IV immediately
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV
quiz.explanation: HIET is the cornerstone treatment for CCB overdose with haemodynamic compromise. Insulin improves cardiac myocyte metabolism independent of receptor binding. Calcium chloride should also be given. Atropine resistance is expected in severe CCB toxicity.

modules.title: Critical Appraisal of RCTs — The FRCEM Examiner's Framework

bullets.text: PICO framework: Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome — the first question in any appraisal; verify the population is comparable to your patient group

Randomisation adequacy: sequence generation (computer random) vs allocation concealment (sealed envelopes, central allocation) — concealment prevents selection bias; sequence generation alone is insufficient
Blinding hierarchy: unblinded < single-blind < double-blind; note when blinding is impossible (e.g., surgical vs drug trials) and assess risk of performance bias

Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis: all patients analysed in assigned group regardless of what they received — preserves randomisation, avoids attrition bias; per-protocol analysis inflates efficacy estimates
Absolute Risk Difference (ARD) and NNT: ARD = Control event rate − Treatment event rate; NNT = 1/ARD — more clinically meaningful than relative risk alone
RR vs OR: when event rate is low (<10%), RR approximately equals OR; when events are common, OR overestimates relative risk — always check which is reported
P-value vs 95% CI: CI width indicates precision and clinical significance; a narrow CI crossing the null = definitively no effect; p-value alone tells you nothing about magnitude

deep_dive.heading: Type I and Type II Errors in Trial Design
points: Type I error (alpha): false positive — declaring an effect that does not exist; convention alpha = 0.05
Type II error (beta): false negative — missing a real effect; convention beta = 0.2, giving power = 80%
Sample size: calculated from alpha, power, and minimum clinically important difference (MCID) — small underpowered trials should be interpreted cautiously
A negative trial (p>0.05) does not mean no effect — it may be underpowered; always inspect the confidence interval
FRCEM exam tip: calculate NNT from absolute risks, not relative values — examiners specifically test this distinction

quiz.question: A trial reports that an intervention reduced mortality from 10% to 8%. The relative risk reduction is 20%. What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT)?
quiz.explanation: ARD = 10% − 8% = 2% (0.02). NNT = 1/ARD = 1/0.02 = 50. The RRR of 20% sounds impressive but the absolute benefit is modest. Examiners expect candidates to calculate from absolute risks, as NNT depends critically on baseline event rate.

source.title: Critical Appraisal Tools — Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine

modules.title: Diagnostic Test Statistics — Sensitivity, Specificity, and Likelihood Ratios

bullets.text: The 2×2 table: rows = disease present/absent, columns = test positive/negative; TP, FP, FN, TN are the building blocks — all statistics derive from this table
Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN): proportion of diseased patients who test positive; SnNout — high sensitivity RULES OUT disease when the test is negative
Specificity = TN/(TN+FP): proportion of non-diseased patients who test negative; SpPin — high specificity RULES IN disease when the test is positive
PPV and NPV are prevalence-dependent: same test has higher PPV in high-prevalence populations — apply in clinical context, not from paper alone
LR+ = Sensitivity/(1−Specificity): LR+ >10 strongly rules in; LR+ 5–10 moderate; LR− <0.1 strongly rules out; LR− 0.1–0.2 moderate
Fagan nomogram: converts pre-test probability + LR to post-test probability — anchor your clinical estimate first, then apply the test result
ROC curve and AUC: perfect discriminator AUC = 1.0; random = 0.5; AUC >0.8 is considered good diagnostic performance

deep_dive.heading: Worked Example: CTPA for PE
points: CTPA sensitivity ~83%, specificity ~96% for PE in clinical trials
LR+ = 0.83/0.04 = 20.75 → strongly rules in PE when positive
LR− = 0.17/0.96 = 0.18 → only moderately rules out PE when negative
Pre-test probability 20%: positive CTPA → post-test ~84%; negative CTPA → post-test ~4%
Pre-test probability 5%: positive CTPA → post-test ~51%; negative CTPA → post-test ~1% — context determines clinical utility

quiz.question: A new bedside test for PE has sensitivity 92% and specificity 45%. Which statement is correct?
options: A positive result strongly rules in PE
A negative result can meaningfully contribute to ruling out PE
The test is only useful when specificity exceeds 90%
Specificity of 45% makes the test clinically useless
quiz.explanation: LR− = (1−0.92)/0.45 = 0.18 — moderately rules out. High sensitivity (SnNout) means a negative result significantly lowers post-test probability. Low specificity (LR+ ~1.6) means a positive result is not helpful. The negative result still has clinical value.
