modules.title: Meta-Analysis and Forest Plots — Reading Pooled Evidence at a Glance

bullets.text: Forest plot anatomy: each horizontal line = one study (length = CI, box size = weight), diamond at bottom = pooled estimate, vertical line = effect null (OR=1 or RD=0)
Heterogeneity: I² statistic — <25% low, 25–75% moderate, >75% high; high I² means pooling may be misleading; investigate clinical reasons
Fixed-effects model: assumes one true effect size; random-effects model: assumes true effect varies between studies — random-effects gives wider, more conservative CI
Publication bias: funnel plot asymmetry suggests positive studies are overrepresented; Egger test provides statistical assessment of asymmetry
GRADE framework: High → Moderate → Low → Very Low quality of evidence; RCTs start as High but downgraded for bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision
Applying NNT from meta-analysis: use UK baseline event rate, not trial population's — pooled OR of 0.70 means very different things at 1% vs 30% baseline risk
PRISMA checklist and PROSPERO pre-registration: quality markers for a systematic review; dual independent screening reduces selection bias

deep_dive.heading: FRCEM Exam Pitfalls in Meta-Analysis Questions
points: The diamond crossing the line of no effect = result is NOT statistically significant — a common exam trap
Wide CI (long diamond) = imprecise estimate from few or small studies — cannot be applied confidently
Pooled OR of 0.80 is NOT the same as 20% absolute risk reduction — convert using baseline event rate
I² >75% means the pooled estimate should be interpreted very cautiously — studies may not be measuring the same construct
A Cochrane review rated GRADE low quality: results are plausible but certainty is limited — guidelines should acknowledge this

quiz.question: A meta-analysis of 8 RCTs shows a pooled OR of 0.72 (95% CI 0.55–0.94, I²=68%) for a new antibiotic in sepsis. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Definitive result — OR 0.72 with CI not crossing 1.0 confirms benefit
High heterogeneity (I²=68%) means the pooled estimate should be interpreted cautiously
The result is statistically significant therefore clinically significant
I²=68% means 68% of studies were biased
quiz.explanation: I²=68% indicates substantial heterogeneity — studies may differ in populations, drug doses, or outcomes. While the CI doesn't cross 1.0 (statistically significant), the variability means the true treatment effect may differ substantially in different patient populations. I² measures heterogeneity, not bias.

source.title: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions

modules.title: Aortic Dissection — ADD-RS, CT Aortogram, and the STEMI Trap

bullets.text: Stanford Type A (ascending aorta involved): surgical emergency; mortality 1–2% per hour without intervention
Stanford Type B (descending only): medical management with beta-blocker + analgesia; surgery/TEVAR if complicated by malperfusion or rupture

ADD-RS (Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score): one point each for high-risk history (abrupt tearing/ripping pain), exam (pulse deficit, BP differential ≥20 mmHg, aortic regurgitation), imaging (mediastinal widening) — score ≥1: CT aortogram

The STEMI trap: inferior STEMI can be caused by Type A dissection occluding the right coronary ostium — thrombolysis is catastrophic; CT aortogram BEFORE any reperfusion therapy if dissection is in the differential
CXR: normal in 12–20% of dissections — mediastinum >8 cm, loss of aortic knuckle, left pleural effusion are supportive but absence does NOT exclude
CT aortogram: investigation of choice, sensitivity/specificity >95% — image from arch to iliac bifurcation; contrast timing is critical
BP and HR control: target systolic 100–120 mmHg and HR <60 — IV labetalol 5–10 mg boluses or esmolol infusion; avoid vasodilators without beta-blockade

deep_dive.heading: Presentations That Masquerade as Other Diagnoses
points: Neurological: carotid involvement causes stroke/TIA; thrombolysing a dissection presenting as stroke is lethal
Abdominal pain: mesenteric artery involvement causes gut ischaemia — dissection extends distally
Limb ischaemia: femoral/iliac involvement — pulseless leg with back pain should raise dissection
Syncope: aortic root haemopericardium → tamponade — BP differential may be absent early
Document explicitly: considering and excluding aortic dissection in chest pain is standard medico-legal practice

quiz.question: A 62-year-old with sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back has BP 170/100 right arm and 140/85 left. ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in II, III, aVF. What is the safest next step?
options: Thrombolysis — this is an inferior STEMI
CT aortogram before any reperfusion therapy
Aspirin 300 mg and heparin bolus
Bedside echo only and proceed to cath lab
quiz.explanation: Tearing back pain and BP differential strongly suggest aortic dissection with right coronary ostium involvement producing an inferior STEMI pattern. Giving thrombolysis to a dissection causes haemorrhagic death. CT aortogram must come first. Primary PCI with cardiac surgery standing by is the only safe approach if dissection is confirmed.

source.title: Aortic Dissection — Emergency Management

modules.title: Myasthenic Crisis — NIF <20 cmH₂O Means Intubate, Not Watch

bullets.text: Myasthenic crisis: severe exacerbation with respiratory muscle failure requiring ventilatory support; common triggers are infection, surgery, and certain drugs
Fatigable weakness: ptosis and diplopia worsening with sustained upgaze, bulbar weakness (dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech), proximal limb weakness — all worsen through the day
Respiratory assessment: NIF (negative inspiratory force) — intubation threshold is NIF <20 cmH2O; also VC <1 L or <20 mL/kg; use the 20-30-40 rule as a bedside guide
Cholinergic crisis (excess pyridostigmine): SLUDGE — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI distress, Emesis + muscle fasciculations — distinguish from myasthenic crisis
Drugs that worsen MG: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers, procainamide — avoid or use with extreme caution
Crisis treatment: stop pyridostigmine (may worsen secretions), IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days OR plasma exchange — both equally effective, plasma exchange has faster onset
Lambert-Eaton (LEMS): proximal limb weakness that IMPROVES with repetitive activity (opposite of MG); 60% paraneoplastic SCLC; anti-VGCC antibodies; check CT chest

deep_dive.heading: RSI in Myasthenia Gravis — Drug Considerations
points: Suxamethonium resistance: ACh receptor upregulation → may require 1.5–2× dose; response is unpredictable
Rocuronium sensitivity: prolonged block expected due to reduced ACh receptor reserve — use 0.6 mg/kg or titrate with nerve stimulator
Sugammadex: reverses rocuronium reliably in MG — have immediately available
Avoid aminoglycosides perioperatively — they block neuromuscular transmission independently
Post-extubation: MG patients at high risk of re-intubation — minimum 24h in HDU/ICU after any intubation

quiz.question: A known myasthenic patient has worsening dysphagia and dysarthria. VC 1.2 L and NIF −18 cmH2O. Which is the correct immediate action?
options: Increase pyridostigmine dose
Prepare for intubation — NIF below threshold with bulbar symptoms indicates imminent respiratory failure
Start oral prednisolone 60 mg
Observe in the ED for 4 hours
quiz.explanation: NIF <20 cmH2O is an intubation threshold in myasthenic crisis. NIF −18 cmH2O combined with VC <1.5 L and bulbar symptoms indicates imminent respiratory failure. Increasing pyridostigmine risks cholinergic crisis. Early elective intubation is far safer than emergency intubation after arrest.

source.title: Myasthenic Crisis — Emergency Management

modules.title: Anaphylaxis — NICE NG258, Three Tryptase Samples, and Biphasic Reactions

bullets.text: Diagnosis (NICE NG258): acute onset + mucocutaneous features ± cardiovascular or respiratory involvement, following likely allergen exposure
Adrenaline 1:1000: 0.5 mg IM (0.5 mL) anterolateral mid-thigh in adults — FIRST treatment always; do NOT delay for antihistamine or steroid; repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement
Paediatric adrenaline doses: >12 years 0.5 mg; 6–12 years 0.3 mg; <6 years 0.15 mg IM — all using 1:1000 preparation
Three mast cell tryptase samples (NG258): 1st at 30–120 min post-onset, 2nd at 3–4h, 3rd baseline >24h or at follow-up — all three are required to confirm diagnosis
Observation period: minimum 6–12h for moderate reactions; 24h if severe, previous biphasic reaction, or laryngeal oedema — biphasic reactions occur in 3–20%, up to 72h later
Steroids NOT recommended routinely in initial management (NICE NG258 2024 update) — no evidence they prevent biphasic reactions; antihistamines also not first-line
Discharge: 2 adrenaline auto-injectors + written action plan + antihistamine/prednisolone course + mandatory allergy referral (NG258 requirement, not optional)

deep_dive.heading: Refractory Anaphylaxis Protocol
steps: After 2 IM adrenaline doses with no improvement: call for critical care help immediately
IV adrenaline: ONLY in cardiac arrest (1 mg bolus) OR in expert setting with monitoring (50 mcg boluses titrated)
Position: supine with legs raised unless airway concern — sitting or standing is linked to empty ventricle syndrome and arrest
IV fluids: 500 mL–1 L crystalloid bolus for distributive shock — may need up to 5–8 L total
Refractory vasodilation: vasopressin 1–2 units IV if noradrenaline infusion is insufficient
Airway: early intubation for laryngeal oedema — oedema progresses rapidly and the window closes

quiz.question: A 32-year-old develops acute urticaria, lip swelling, and wheeze after eating peanuts. BP 90/60. Which is the correct first drug and route?
options: Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV — antihistamine first
Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV — steroid to prevent biphasic reaction
Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh
Salbutamol nebuliser 5 mg for the wheeze
quiz.explanation: IM adrenaline is ALWAYS the first-line treatment in anaphylaxis. NICE NG258 is explicit — do not delay adrenaline for antihistamines or steroids. IM into the anterolateral thigh achieves faster absorption than the deltoid. Salbutamol is an adjunct, not a primary treatment for anaphylaxis.

source.title: Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment (NG258)

modules.title: Meningitis and Encephalitis — Antibiotics Before CT, Always

bullets.text: Classic triad of bacterial meningitis (headache, neck stiffness, photophobia) is present in only 44% of cases — absence does not exclude the diagnosis
Jolt accentuation test (headache worsening with 2–3 Hz horizontal head rotation): sensitivity 97% for meningism — more sensitive than Kernig's or Brudzinski's
CT before LP indications: GCS <13, focal neurology, papilloedema, new seizure, immunosuppression, known CNS lesion — in ALL other cases, LP first
Antibiotics MUST NOT be delayed for CT: give ceftriaxone 2 g IV (adult) immediately when LP is deferred; delay >30 min worsens mortality
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV (max 10 mg) with or just before first antibiotic dose: reduces mortality (NNT ~8) and deafness in bacterial meningitis
HSV encephalitis: temporal lobe involvement on MRI DWI, EEG periodic complexes, CSF PCR; give aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8h empirically while awaiting results
CSF interpretation: bacterial (PMN >100, protein >1 g/L, glucose ratio <0.4), viral (lymphocytes, normal glucose), TB (lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein)

deep_dive.heading: Meningitis Action Sequence
steps: Recognition: fever + headache + any neurological sign — assume meningitis until excluded
Immediate: blood cultures × 2, then ceftriaxone 2 g IV — do NOT wait for CT or LP
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV simultaneously with or just before first antibiotic dose
CT head only if one of the indications above is present, then LP — collect 10–15 mL CSF in 3 numbered bottles
Add aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV if encephalitis features (altered cognition, behavioural change, focal deficit)
UKHSA notification immediately for confirmed meningococcal — ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO single dose for close contacts

quiz.question: A 22-year-old has fever 39.2°C, severe headache for 6 hours, and neck stiffness. GCS 15, no focal neurology, no papilloedema. What is the correct sequence?
options: CT head first, then LP if normal, then antibiotics
LP immediately (no CT indicated), then ceftriaxone + dexamethasone
Blood cultures then ceftriaxone + dexamethasone immediately, then LP (no CT indication present)
Oral antibiotics and GP follow-up if clinically stable
quiz.explanation: With GCS 15, no focal neurology, no papilloedema, there is NO indication for CT before LP. Correct sequence: blood cultures → ceftriaxone 2 g IV + dexamethasone → then LP. Do not delay antibiotics even to perform the LP first.

source.title: Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal septicaemia in under 16s (CG102)

modules.title: Life-Threatening Rashes — Diagnoses That Cannot Wait for Dermatology

bullets.text: Meningococcal septicaemia: non-blanching petechiae/purpura — glass test; benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV immediately; do not wait for bloods; call critical care now
SJS vs TEN: SJS <10% BSA skin detachment, TEN >30%, overlap 10–30%; positive Nikolsky sign (skin detaches with lateral pressure); mucous membrane involvement is key
SJS/TEN drug causes: allopurinol (most common in UK), carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulphonamides, oxicam NSAIDs — stop the causative drug immediately
SSSS vs TEN: SSSS — intraepidermal cleavage (superficial, heals well); TEN — subepidermal cleavage (full-thickness, scarring) — skin biopsy differentiates if uncertain
Necrotising fasciitis: pain out of proportion, crepitus, skin blistering, gas on imaging; LRINEC score ≥8 = high risk; immediate surgical referral — imaging must not delay theatre
Toxic Shock Syndrome: Strep TSS (hypotension + soft tissue infection + organ failure); treat with clindamycin (inhibits toxin production) + beta-lactam; remove focus
Purpura fulminans: severe DIC with symmetrical acral necrosis in meningococcal/asplenic patients; FFP and prompt antimicrobials; immediate ICU admission

deep_dive.heading: SJS/TEN — ED Management Principles
points: Stop all non-essential drugs immediately — identify the most likely causative drug using a medication timeline
Fluid resuscitation as for burns patient: substantial losses through denuded skin
Strict temperature control: patients cannot thermoregulate through damaged skin
Urgent ophthalmology review: eye involvement is frequent and can cause permanent blindness
Refer to burns unit or specialist dermatology centre — management complexity equivalent to major burns

quiz.question: A 45-year-old started allopurinol 6 weeks ago with fever, painful erythema on face and trunk, oral ulcers, and conjunctivitis. Skin detaches when lateral pressure applied. What is the immediate priority?
options: Topical steroids and dermatology outpatient referral
Stop allopurinol, urgent admission, consider burns/dermatology unit transfer
IV aciclovir for disseminated herpes simplex
Emollients and discharge with oral antihistamines
quiz.explanation: This is SJS/TEN — allopurinol is the most common drug cause in the UK. Positive Nikolsky sign + mucosal involvement + drug exposure confirms the diagnosis. Causative drug must be stopped immediately. Specialist inpatient management equivalent to burns care is required.

source.title: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis

modules.title: HOCM in the ED — What Not to Give Is as Important as What to Give

bullets.text: Pathophysiology: asymmetric septal hypertrophy → dynamic LVOT obstruction; systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve worsens obstruction in high-flow states
ECG: LVH voltage criteria, deep Q waves in lateral (I, aVL) and inferior leads, apical HOCM variant shows giant symmetric T-wave inversion V4–V6 (Yamaguchi pattern)
Clinical: exertional syncope (Valsalva physiology), dyspnoea, angina; crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur INCREASES with Valsalva and DECREASES with squatting (opposite of fixed AS)
Treatment: beta-blockers (bisoprolol, metoprolol) and verapamil — reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, reduce dynamic obstruction
Contraindicated in HOCM: nitrates, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, inotropes — all reduce preload or SVR, worsening obstruction; nitrates can cause catastrophic haemodynamic collapse
Acute decompensation: IV phenylephrine (alpha-agonist) to raise SVR; passive leg raise; IV beta-blockers for rate control; avoid tachycardia absolutely
Sudden cardiac death: leading cause in young UK athletes <35; ICD for survivors of VF, those with family history of SCD, or high-risk feature on cardiac imaging

deep_dive.heading: HOCM Murmur — Bedside Manoeuvres
points: Valsalva (straining): reduces venous return → decreased preload → increased obstruction → murmur gets LOUDER
Squatting: increases venous return → increased preload → decreased obstruction → murmur gets SOFTER
Standing quickly: same as Valsalva — murmur louder; useful bedside test
Aortic stenosis: fixed obstruction, murmur relatively unchanged by these manoeuvres
This dynamic physiology explains why nitrates are so dangerous — they mimic Valsalva by reducing preload

quiz.question: A 22-year-old footballer collapses during training. ECG shows LVH and deep Q waves in I and aVL. Echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy. BP 105/70, HR 110. Which drug should be given?
options: GTN sublingual for possible angina
Furosemide 40 mg IV for possible pulmonary oedema
IV metoprolol 5 mg for rate control and obstruction reduction
Dobutamine infusion for cardiac output support
quiz.explanation: HOCM with tachycardia requires rate reduction to increase diastolic filling and reduce dynamic obstruction. IV beta-blockers achieve this safely. GTN, furosemide, and dobutamine are all contraindicated — they reduce preload or increase contractility/HR, potentially causing fatal haemodynamic collapse.

source.title: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM)

modules.title: Carbon Monoxide — The Great Mimic and the SpO2 That Lies

bullets.text: Mechanism: CO has 240× higher affinity for haemoglobin than O2; COHb shifts O2 dissociation curve left; CO also binds cytochrome oxidase, blocking cellular respiration
Presentation: headache, nausea, cognitive impairment, vomiting — cherry-red skin is a LATE and rare autopsy finding; flu-like illness with no fever is the classic ED presentation
SpO2 pulse oximetry is falsely NORMAL — cannot distinguish COHb from oxyhaemoglobin; only co-oximetry ABG correctly measures COHb level
COHb levels: <10% mild (headache); 10–20% moderate (headache, vomiting); 20–40% severe (confusion, syncope); >40% loss of consciousness, seizures, cardiac arrest
High-flow O2: 100% FiO2 via non-rebreathe mask reduces COHb half-life from ~5h (on air) to 60–90 min — start immediately; continue until COHb <5% and asymptomatic
HBO UK indications: COHb >25%, any loss of consciousness, neurological deficit, cardiac involvement (ECG changes, arrhythmia), pregnancy (any COHb level) — contact national HBO centre
Delayed neurological sequelae (DNS): cognitive and personality changes 2–6 weeks post-exposure; COHb at time of treatment does not predict risk; refer to neurology

deep_dive.heading: Public Health Actions After CO Presentation
steps: Identify source: faulty boiler, gas appliance, log burner, car exhaust in enclosed space — fire service must attend property
Household contacts: all present at time of exposure must attend ED for COHb testing regardless of symptoms
Refer to UKHSA/local public health team for household CO alarm fitting follow-up
Screen for intentional exposure vs accidental — safeguarding implications if children involved
Pets: small animals affected earlier than humans — a dead canary or gerbil is a historical but relevant clue
Document: time of discovery, source, estimated duration of exposure, number of persons affected — all affect prognostication

quiz.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman (12 weeks) is brought in from a house with a faulty boiler. She is alert, COHb 18% on co-oximetry ABG. SpO2 is 99% on air. What is the correct management?
options: SpO2 is normal — discharge with CO alarm advice
High-flow O2 and arrange HBO regardless of COHb level in pregnancy
Standard O2 therapy only — HBO is contraindicated in pregnancy
COHb 18% is below HBO threshold — observe and discharge
quiz.explanation: In pregnancy, ANY detectable COHb level is an indication for HBO — fetal haemoglobin has even higher CO affinity and fetal CO elimination is slower. HBO is NOT contraindicated in pregnancy. The apparently normal SpO2 demonstrates the oximetry trap — always use co-oximetry ABG in suspected CO poisoning.

source.title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

modules.title: BRUE — Brief Resolved Unexplained Events: Low-Risk vs High-Risk

bullets.text: BRUE definition (AAP 2016): infant <1 year, sudden brief episode <1 minute, now resolved, with no explanation, and ≥1 of: colour change (cyanosis/pallor), irregular/absent breathing, tone change, altered responsiveness
Low-risk criteria (all must be met): age >60 days, gestational age ≥38 weeks, FIRST BRUE, NO CPR required by trained clinician, no concerning features on exam or history
Low-risk BRUE: recommend AGAINST routine bloods, ECG, EEG, imaging, or septic workup — brief observation and parental education is appropriate; this is evidence-based, not negligent
Recurrence rate: 9–14%; serious underlying diagnosis found in up to 5% of all BRUEs — mimics must be excluded by careful history and examination

BRUE mimics: GI causes (30%) — GORD, oesophageal dysmotility; respiratory (12%) — pertussis, RSV; neurological — seizures; cardiac — long QT, SVT; metabolic — hypoglycaemia; child maltreatment (~2–3%)
High-risk features requiring admission and workup: age <60 days, prematurity, recurrent BRUE, CPR given by trained clinician, abnormal exam, concerning social history
Always: consider non-accidental injury, document parental concern, assess feeding and growth, check social circumstances — safeguarding is implicit in every BRUE assessment

deep_dive.heading: BRUE Assessment Framework
steps: History: exact sequence of events, witness account, feeding position, duration, recovery — establish BRUE vs not-unexplained
Examination: weight centile, tone, fontanelle, bruising/petechiae, eye exam — signs of NAI or systemic disease
Low-risk criteria all met: brief ED observation, parent education on infant CPR, safety netting — no routine investigations required
High-risk or uncertain: admit, ECG (long QT screen), monitored bed, targeted investigations based on clinical suspicion
ECG: QTc >460 ms warrants paediatric cardiology review; always calculate corrected QT using Bazett formula
Safeguarding: BRUE with social concerns, unexplained marks, or implausible history → MASH/CP referral before discharge

quiz.question: A 3-month-old full-term infant had a 20-second episode of pallor and limpness while feeding, witnessed by the mother. She recovered immediately. First such episode, no CPR given, examination is normal. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Full septic workup and 48h admission
Discharge with no investigation — this is a low-risk BRUE
Brief ED observation, parent education on infant CPR, safety netting — no routine investigations
EEG and head MRI before any discharge decision
quiz.explanation: This meets low-risk BRUE criteria (>60 days, term, first episode, no CPR by clinician, normal exam). AAP 2016 guidelines recommend against routine investigations. Brief observation with parent education and safety-netting is appropriate and evidence-based.

source.title: Emergency medicine updates: Pediatric brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE)

modules.title: Rocuronium for RSI — Why >1.2 mg/kg Improves First-Pass Success

bullets.text: Rocuronium >1.2 mg/kg significantly improves first-attempt intubation success — a 2026 retrospective analysis in ED and ICU settings (Am J Emerg Med, PMID 42385663) confirms this dose-response relationship
Standard intubating dose 1.2 mg/kg (3× ED95): onset 60–90 seconds; the traditional 0.6 mg/kg (1× ED95) is inadequate for RSI — do not use doses <1.2 mg/kg
For maximum onset speed: 1.6 mg/kg provides conditions comparable to suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg at 90 seconds — use when aspiration risk is highest
Suxamethonium vs rocuronium: suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg has fastest onset (45–60s) and shortest duration (8–10 min) — preferred for anticipated difficult airway where wake-up may be needed
Rocuronium advantages: no hyperkalaemia risk (safe in burns >24h, denervation, severe AKI), no malignant hyperthermia trigger, no fasciculations
Duration: rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg lasts 35–45 min; 1.6 mg/kg lasts 60–90 min — plan post-intubation sedation before pushing the paralytic
Sugammadex 16 mg/kg IV reverses rocuronium within 3–5 minutes — must be immediately available in every resus bay as the plan B for CICO on rocuronium

deep_dive.heading: Rocuronium or Suxamethonium — Decision Framework
points: Default for most RSIs: rocuronium 1.2–1.6 mg/kg — fewer absolute contraindications, reversal available with sugammadex
Choose suxamethonium: known/predicted difficult airway where wake-up is desirable, no hyperkalaemia risk, no MH history
Absolute suxamethonium contraindications: hyperkalaemia, burns/crush >24h, denervation syndromes, myopathies, personal/FH malignant hyperthermia
High-risk rocuronium: myasthenia gravis (unpredictable block), severe hepatic failure (prolonged duration)
KETAMINE-RSI trial (NEJM 2026, PMID 41369227): no mortality difference between ketamine and etomidate — induction drug choice should reflect individual haemodynamics

quiz.question: A 65-year-old with advanced CKD (K+ 6.2 mmol/L) requires emergency intubation. Which neuromuscular blocking agent is most appropriate?
options: Suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg — fastest onset
Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg — no hyperkalaemia risk, reversible with sugammadex
Vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg
No paralytic — awake fibreoptic intubation only
quiz.explanation: Suxamethonium causes rapid K+ release from depolarised muscle — in a patient with K+ 6.2 mmol/L this risks fatal hyperkalaemia and VF. Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg provides reliable RSI conditions without this risk and can be rapidly reversed with sugammadex 16 mg/kg if needed.

source.title: Rocuronium dosing for rapid sequence intubation: A retrospective analysis in ED and ICU settings

modules.title: Febrile Infant 60–90 Days — IBI Risk 1.1% and How to Stratify

bullets.text: A 2026 JAMA Pediatrics meta-analysis (PMID 42189531) reports pooled IBI prevalence of 1.11% in well-appearing febrile infants aged 60–90 days — bacteraemia accounts for most; bacterial meningitis is rare
The 60–90 day age group sits between definitely high risk (<60 days) and likely viral (>90 days) — structured risk stratification, not uniform LP/admission, is the evidence-based approach
NICE NG143 and Step-by-Step algorithm: procalcitonin, CRP, ANC, and NICE traffic light appearance all contribute to risk classification in this age group
Low-risk features: well-appearing, procalcitonin <0.5 ng/mL, negative urine dipstick, ANC <10×10⁹/L — can be managed with close safety-netting and early return review
High-risk features: ill-appearing, petechiae, temperature >39°C (>38°C if <3 months), procalcitonin ≥0.5 ng/mL, ANC >10×10⁹/L — warrant blood cultures, urine MC&S, empirical antibiotics
UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection in this age group — catheter specimen urine or suprapubic aspiration is more reliable than dipstick alone in infants
Empirical antibiotic: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV OD covers E. coli and GBS; add ampicillin if Listeria risk; always take cultures before giving antibiotics

deep_dive.heading: Step-by-Step Risk Stratification for Febrile Infant 60–90 Days
steps: Appearance: ill-appearing = high risk, admit regardless of all other markers
Urine dipstick: leucocytes/nitrites positive → likely UTI, treat empirically pending cultures
Procalcitonin: ≥0.5 ng/mL = elevated risk; increases IBI probability significantly
CRP: >20 mg/L is a red flag in this age group alongside other markers
ANC: ≥10×10⁹/L = neutrophilia, adds to high-risk classification
Low risk (all negative, well-appearing): shared decision-making with parents, review at 12–24h, written safety-net advice with clear return guidance

quiz.question: A 72-day-old well-appearing full-term infant has temperature 38.4°C. Urine dipstick negative, procalcitonin 0.3 ng/mL, CRP 8 mg/L, ANC 6×10⁹/L. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Full septic workup including LP and empirical antibiotics
Discharge immediately — no risk factors identified
Apply Step-by-Step criteria: low-risk category may allow discharge with close safety-netting and early review
Admit for 48 hours observation regardless of risk stratification
quiz.explanation: This infant meets Step-by-Step low-risk criteria (well-appearing, negative urine, procalcitonin <0.5, normal ANC, low CRP). Validated risk stratification allows selective investigation and managed discharge with close follow-up, avoiding over-medicalisation while ensuring safety.

source.title: Prevalence of Invasive Bacterial Infections Among Febrile Infants Aged 60 to 90 Days

modules.title: Pulmonary Embolism — Intermediate-High Risk: When Anticoagulation Alone Is Not Enough

bullets.text: PE risk stratification: massive (cardiac arrest/refractory shock) → thrombolyse or ECMO; intermediate-high (RV dysfunction + troponin rise, haemodynamically stable) → escalation consideration; low risk (sPESI 0) → outpatient DOAC

STORM-PE RCT (Circulation 2026, PMID 41183181): catheter-directed aspiration/vacuum thrombectomy (CAVT) vs anticoagulation alone — CAVT superior for RV/LV ratio reduction at 48h with comparable adverse events
POCUS for PE: RV:LV ratio >1.0 in 4-chamber view, D-sign (septal flattening), McConnell sign (RV free wall akinesis with spared apex) — confirm RV dysfunction and escalate risk tier
Thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2h): for massive PE only; PEITHO trial shows intermediate-risk thrombolysis increases major bleeding and stroke — NOT routine practice
DOAC outpatient PE: sPESI 0 + HESTIA criteria met → outpatient apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD is safe; admission does not improve outcomes in sPESI 0-1 (PMID 42313763)
PE response team: intermediate-high risk PE requires multidisciplinary input (cardiology, interventional radiology, haematology) — most UK centres now have dedicated PE response teams
All PE: anticoagulate immediately with LMWH or DOAC loading dose before/during imaging confirmation unless haemorrhagic contraindication

deep_dive.heading: PE Risk Stratification to Treatment Pathway
steps: Haemodynamic instability (SBP <90 or cardiac arrest)? Yes → massive PE: systemic thrombolysis 100 mg alteplase over 2h (50 mg if in arrest)
Stable but RV dysfunction on echo + elevated troponin? → Intermediate-high: anticoagulate, HDU, activate PE response team for CAVT discussion
Stable, no RV dysfunction, troponin negative? → Intermediate-low: anticoagulate and observe
sPESI 0 + HESTIA criteria met? → Low risk: outpatient DOAC, apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days
All PE: anticoagulate before imaging completion if clinical diagnosis is strong
CTPA remains gold standard; VQ scan preferred in CKD/contrast allergy

quiz.question: A 55-year-old has confirmed PE on CTPA. HR 108, BP 118/76, SpO2 94% on 2L O2. Echo shows RV:LV ratio 1.3 and D-sign. Troponin I elevated at 120 ng/L. Which is most appropriate?
options: Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours) immediately
Discharge with DOAC — sPESI likely 0
Intermediate-high risk PE: anticoagulate, HDU admission, activate PE response team for CAVT consideration
Repeat echo in 24h then decide
quiz.explanation: RV dysfunction (RV:LV >1.0) with elevated troponin = intermediate-high risk PE. Patient is haemodynamically stable so immediate thrombolysis is not indicated (PEITHO: increased bleeding without mortality benefit in this subgroup). Anticoagulation, close monitoring, and PE team for possible CAVT is correct.

source.title: STORM-PE Trial — Mechanical Thrombectomy vs Anticoagulation in Intermediate-High Risk PE

modules.title: Sepsis 2026 — Updated Guidelines, Capillary Refill Targets, and Vasopressor Escalation

bullets.text: Sepsis definition (Sepsis-3): life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by dysregulated host response to infection — SOFA score ≥2 change from baseline; qSOFA ≥2 for rapid screening outside ICU
Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics, IV antibiotics within 1 hour for septic shock, crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, vasopressors if MAP <65 after fluids, remeasure lactate

ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 RCT (JAMA 2025, PMID 41159835): capillary refill time (CRT)-guided personalised resuscitation was superior to usual care — CRT is now validated as a resuscitation target alongside MAP and lactate
Antibiotic choice: piperacillin/tazobactam (Tazocin) 4.5 g IV TDS or meropenem 1 g IV TDS for undifferentiated septic shock; escalate to meropenem if ESBL risk or no response at 48h
Vasopressor sequence (Surviving Sepsis 2026): noradrenaline first-line; add vasopressin 0.03 units/min when noradrenaline ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min; hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for refractory shock
Fluid strategy 2026: against fixed 30 mL/kg bolus in all patients — dynamic assessment (passive leg raise, pulse pressure variation) preferred; avoid fluid overload
Source control within 6–12 hours of identification (drain abscess, remove infected device) — delay beyond 12h independently associated with worse outcomes

deep_dive.heading: ED Septic Shock Resuscitation Algorithm
steps: 0–15 min: recognise (NEWS2 ≥7, lactate ≥2, suspected infection), blood cultures × 2, broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately
0–30 min: 250–500 mL crystalloid boluses with reassessment after each; MAP target ≥65 mmHg
If MAP <65 after 1–2 L crystalloid: start noradrenaline via peripheral IV (up to 1–2h peripherally while CVC placed)
Reassess dynamically: CRT, HR, MAP, lactate, urine output — dynamic measures outperform static CVP
Escalating vasopressor need (noradrenaline >0.25 mcg/kg/min): add vasopressin 0.03 units/min + hydrocortisone 200 mg/24h
Source control: identify and treat source within 12h; imaging to exclude drainable collection

quiz.question: A 70-year-old with suspected urinary source sepsis has MAP 58 despite 1.5 L crystalloid. HR 118, CRT 5 seconds, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. What is the next most important intervention?
options: Give another 1 L crystalloid bolus before considering vasopressors
Start noradrenaline targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg
Await blood culture results before starting antibiotics
Give furosemide 40 mg IV to prevent fluid overload
quiz.explanation: This is septic shock with persistent hypotension after adequate fluid resuscitation and a rising lactate. Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor and should start without further delay. Antibiotics should already have been given. Furosemide is absolutely contraindicated in distributive shock.

source.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines 2026

modules.title: Paediatric Septic Shock Fluids — SQUEAKY Trial: Balanced Crystalloid or Saline?

bullets.text: PALISI SQUEAKY trial (NEJM 2026, PMID 42028918): 47 EDs across 5 countries, children with septic shock — balanced crystalloid vs 0.9% saline — NO significant difference in death, new RRT, or persistent kidney dysfunction
The theoretical harm of normal saline (hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, renal vasoconstriction) did not translate to clinical outcome difference in this large paediatric study
Adult data (SMART, SALT-ED): balanced crystalloids showed modest AKI benefits in adults — still used preferentially in adults; paediatric evidence is now less clear-cut
Current practice post-SQUEAKY: either fluid type is acceptable in paediatric septic shock; use what is available; never delay resuscitation to obtain balanced crystalloid
Volume matters more than type: reassess after every 10 mL/kg bolus; total 40–60 mL/kg before vasopressor consideration; watch for fluid overload (hepatomegaly, crackles, gallop rhythm)
Children with CHD, DKA, or severe malnutrition: follow disease-specific pathways — standard fluid bolus approach does NOT apply
Vasopressors in paediatric septic shock: adrenaline first-line for warm distributive shock; noradrenaline reasonable; dopamine no longer recommended as first-line (NEJM)

deep_dive.heading: Monitoring Fluid Response in Children
points: HR, capillary refill time (<2s normal, 3–5s delayed, >5s very prolonged), skin mottling, peripheral vs central temperature gap
AVPU or GCS: improving neurological status after fluid suggests adequate perfusion improvement
Liver edge palpation: tender hepatomegaly or increased liver span suggests right heart fluid overload
Lactate: >4 mmol/L higher risk; trend more important than single value; aim to clear lactate over 6h
Urine output: >0.5–1 mL/kg/h in children; absence after 40 mL/kg + vasopressors = RRT discussion

quiz.question: A 5-year-old with septic shock has received 20 mL/kg Plasmalyte. HR 155, CRT 4 seconds. Only 0.9% saline is available. What is the correct approach?
options: Delay resuscitation until Plasmalyte is obtained — saline causes renal injury
Give next bolus of 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline — SQUEAKY trial shows no outcome difference
Switch to albumin — 0.9% saline is contraindicated in children
Start vasopressors now — 20 mL/kg is the maximum safe bolus
quiz.explanation: The SQUEAKY trial (NEJM 2026) found no significant difference between balanced crystalloid and 0.9% saline in paediatric septic shock. Clinical resuscitation should never be delayed for fluid type. Continue with available fluid and reassess after each bolus.

source.title: Balanced Fluid or 0.9% Saline in Children Treated for Septic Shock

modules.title: Major Haemorrhage — MHP Activation, 1:1:1 Ratios, and the Whole Blood Trial

bullets.text: MHP activation criteria: SBP <90, HR >120, transfusion >4 units pRBC in 4h, or clinical exsanguination — activate early; blood products lose the race to crystalloid if called late
1:1:1 ratio (pRBC:FFP:platelets): haemostatic resuscitation addresses coagulopathy from the outset — standard UK MHP practice; avoid large-volume crystalloid which worsens dilutional coagulopathy

Prehospital whole blood RCT (NEJM 2026, PMID 41841706, NHS Blood and Transplant): 2 units prehospital whole blood vs standard care — primary outcome (death/massive transfusion at 24h) NOT significantly different
FFP-first approach (J Trauma 2026, PMID 42275580): FFP as first product in MHP independently associated with improved survival — supports FFP-first over pRBC-first strategy in MHP
Viscoelastic assays (TEG/ROTEM): guides targeted factor replacement; fibrinogen concentrate for hypofibrinogenaemia; increasingly available at UK major trauma centres
Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90 mmHg) until surgical haemostasis: reduce crystalloid before haemorrhage control; AVOID permissive hypotension if TBI is concurrent — target MAP ≥80
Calcium replacement: packed red cells contain citrate; give calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV after every 4 units of blood products to maintain ionised Ca ≥1.1 mmol/L

deep_dive.heading: MHP Activation — Initial Steps
steps: Activate MHP: call blood bank with patient ID and MHP activate — ensure crossmatch blood or O-neg ready
Pack 1: 4 units pRBC + 4 units FFP — administer simultaneously
Mechanical haemostasis: tourniquet or wound packing for compressible haemorrhage — do this first
TXA 1g IV over 10 min within 3h of injury — give concurrently
Calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV after every 4 units of blood products
Target: ionised Ca ≥1.1, fibrinogen ≥1.5 g/L — give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate if low

quiz.question: A 25-year-old stab wound victim has SBP 82, HR 132 after 1L crystalloid. MHP activated. Which statement about blood product ratios is correct?
options: Give 4 more litres of crystalloid before releasing blood products
pRBC only until haemostasis achieved — FFP delays red cell delivery
1:1:1 pRBC:FFP:platelets from MHP pack is the standard haemostatic approach
Whole blood is proven superior and should be the first product
quiz.explanation: 1:1:1 haemostatic resuscitation is the standard UK MHP practice. Large-volume crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy. Prehospital whole blood showed non-inferiority but not superiority in the 2026 NHS NEJM trial. FFP-first has some supporting evidence but standard MHP packs deliver 1:1:1 simultaneously.

source.title: Prehospital Whole Blood in Traumatic Hemorrhage — A Randomized Controlled Trial

modules.title: POCUS for Acute Dyspnoea — Early Diagnostic Certainty at the Bedside

bullets.text: POCUS-driven pathway (Eur J Emerg Med 2026, PMID 41870288): increases early diagnostic certainty in ED dyspnoea; higher concordance between initial and final diagnosis in the POCUS-first group
Lung POCUS for APO: bilateral B-lines (>3 per zone in ≥3 zones bilaterally) — sensitivity 85%, specificity 92% for acute pulmonary oedema vs COPD/asthma
Lung sliding present: pneumothorax excluded at probe position (100% NPV); absent sliding: possible pneumothorax — confirm with M-mode (seashore vs stratosphere sign)
International POCUS lung ultrasound update (ICM 2026, PMID 42257880): now recommended as first-line in acute dyspnoea in experienced hands, before CXR
Cardiac windows: assess LV function, RV:LV ratio, pericardial effusion; 4-chamber view guides real-time fluid management and disposition decisions
IVC assessment: <1 cm collapsing with inspiration = volume-responsive; >2 cm non-collapsing = consider tamponade, RV failure, or tension pneumothorax in context
POCUS does NOT replace formal echo: documents point-of-care answer to specific questions — document what was asked and found; label clips with date, patient ID, view

deep_dive.heading: Lung POCUS Zones and Interpretation
points: 8-zone protocol: 2 anterior + 2 lateral per side; A-lines = normal aeration or pneumothorax (contextual)
B-lines (rocket sign): vertical hyperechoic lines reaching screen edge, erasing A-lines, moving with lung = interstitial fluid
Consolidation: tissue-like echogenicity replacing aerated lung; dynamic air bronchogram = pneumonia (vs static = obstruction)
Free pleural fluid: anechoic space between chest wall and lung — easily measurable, guide for thoracocentesis
Combine cardiac + lung + IVC views for maximum diagnostic yield in undifferentiated dyspnoea

quiz.question: A 72-year-old in respiratory distress has bilateral B-lines in 6 of 8 zones, dilated non-collapsing IVC, and severely impaired LV systolic function on POCUS. Which diagnosis and treatment is correct?
options: Pneumonia — give IV antibiotics
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — IV furosemide 40–80 mg and GTN
Tension pneumothorax — immediate needle decompression
Pulmonary embolism — start anticoagulation
quiz.explanation: Bilateral B-lines + impaired LV + dilated IVC = acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Immediate treatment: IV furosemide and GTN. POCUS allows this diagnosis within 2 minutes. Tension pneumothorax shows absent lung sliding with no B-lines. PE would show RV strain, not LV dysfunction.

source.title: International evidence-based recommendations for point-of-care lung ultrasound: 2025 focused update

modules.title: Upper GI Bleeding — Glasgow-Blatchford, Lactate, and When to Scope Urgently

bullets.text: UGIB mortality predictors (J Emerg Med 2026, PMID 41863907): admission lactate, haemodynamic instability, and active endoscopic bleeding are the strongest early ED mortality predictors — integrate with Glasgow-Blatchford Score

Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS): ≤1 = very low risk, suitable for outpatient endoscopy; ≥12 = high risk, urgent endoscopy within 12–24h; calculates from Urea, Hb, SBP, HR, melaena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure
Haemodynamic resuscitation: pRBC transfusion target Hb >70 g/L (>80 g/L if cardiovascular disease); restrictive transfusion strategy associated with better outcomes in UGIB
IV PPI: pantoprazole or omeprazole 40 mg IV before endoscopy — reduces high-risk endoscopic stigmata; does NOT reduce mortality but reduces re-bleeding and surgery need
Terlipressin 2 mg IV (variceal bleed): first-line vasoactive drug for suspected variceal haemorrhage; continue 1 mg QDS for up to 5 days; ceftriaxone 1 g IV OD mandatory for SBP prophylaxis
Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube: balloon tamponade for uncontrolled variceal bleeding as a bridge to TIPSS — last resort, risk of oesophageal necrosis and aspiration
Document medication review explicitly: NSAIDs, aspirin (unless specific cardiac indication), anticoagulants, and steroids should not be initiated empirically in acute UGIB

deep_dive.heading: UGIB Pathway — Variceal vs Non-Variceal
steps: Stabilise: 2 large-bore IVs, group and screen, consider early intubation for GCS ≤8 or massive ongoing haemorrhage before endoscopy
Non-variceal: IV PPI, transfuse to Hb ≥70, GBS ≥12 or haemodynamic instability → urgent endoscopy within 12h
Variceal suspected (cirrhosis, portal hypertension signs): terlipressin + ceftriaxone immediately, GI/hepatology referral
GBS 0–1: discharge with outpatient endoscopy in 24–72h — validated as safe and cost-effective
Anticoagulated patients: do not routinely reverse unless life-threatening haemorrhage — discuss haematology
Post-endoscopy: Forrest class Ia/Ib (active bleeding) or IIa (visible vessel) → endoscopic therapy + admit

quiz.question: A 58-year-old with known cirrhosis presents with haematemesis, HR 118, BP 92/60. Lactate 5.8 mmol/L. Which is the most important immediate pharmacological intervention?
options: IV PPI (pantoprazole 40 mg)
Terlipressin 2 mg IV and ceftriaxone 1 g IV
Vasopressin 20 units IV bolus
FFP for coagulopathy correction
quiz.explanation: In a cirrhotic with haematemesis and shock, variceal haemorrhage must be assumed. Terlipressin reduces portal pressure and variceal bleeding. Ceftriaxone prophylaxis is mandatory — infection-related mortality is significant in variceal bleeding. IV PPI is not the priority here.

source.title: Emergency Department Predictors of Mortality in Upper GI Bleeding

modules.title: Paediatric MSK Analgesia — Ibuprofen Alone Is Sufficient; Opioids Add Harm

bullets.text: JAMA 2026 RCT (PMID 41505155): in children with acute non-operative MSK injury — ibuprofen plus paracetamol did NOT improve pain at 60 min vs ibuprofen alone; adverse events were 4× higher with hydromorphone
Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg PO (max 400 mg) is first-line for paediatric MSK injury — start at triage before doctor review when possible
Adding paracetamol 15 mg/kg provides no additional analgesia in acute fracture/sprain at 60 min — may still be used for antipyresis or home analgesia after discharge
Oral opioids: no clinically meaningful benefit over ibuprofen alone for non-operative MSK injury, with 4× more adverse events (vomiting, sedation) — avoid routinely
Reserve IV morphine or oral oxycodone for: severe pain, operative fractures, or when oral route is unavailable — use with consent and monitoring
Intranasal fentanyl 1.5 mcg/kg: effective procedural analgesia for fracture reduction without IV access — onset 5–10 min
Regional anaesthesia in the paediatric ED: femoral nerve block for femoral fractures, haematoma block for radius — increasingly available, opioid-sparing, evidence-based

deep_dive.heading: Pain Assessment and Triage Analgesia in Children
points: Pain assessment tools: <4 years FLACC scale, 4–12 years Faces scale, >12 years NRS 0–10
Triage analgesia: empower nurses to administer paracetamol/ibuprofen at triage — reduces time-to-analgesia from ~60 to ~15 minutes
Splinting before X-ray: reduces pain and distress without interfering with the diagnostic image
COMFORT measures: distraction, positioning, carer presence — non-pharmacological analgesia is evidence-based
Discharge: alternating NSAID + paracetamol every 4h is an effective home regimen; codeine NOT recommended in children <12 (CYP2D6 ultra-metaboliser risk)

quiz.question: A 9-year-old has a closed radius fracture. Pain score 7/10. No IV access yet. Which analgesic regimen is most evidence-based for the ED?
options: Wait for IV access before giving any analgesia
Oral ibuprofen 10 mg/kg — as effective as combination therapy for acute paediatric fracture pain
Oral codeine 1 mg/kg — standard opioid for paediatric fractures
Oral paracetamol + ibuprofen simultaneously — combination superior to either alone
quiz.explanation: JAMA 2026 (PMID 41505155) showed ibuprofen alone was as effective as ibuprofen + paracetamol or ibuprofen + opioid in paediatric MSK injury, with fewer adverse events. Codeine is not recommended in children under 12. Combination analgesia is not superior and adds side effects.

source.title: Acetaminophen or Opioid Analgesia Added to Ibuprofen for Children's Musculoskeletal Injury

modules.title: Rib Fractures — Serratus Anterior Plane Block and Regional Analgesia in the ED

bullets.text: SAPB RCT (Acad Emerg Med 2026, PMID 42159402): SAPB added to usual care produced statistically significant pain improvement in ED patients with rib fractures — safe and feasible by emergency physicians

SAPB anatomy: LA injected deep to serratus anterior at the midaxillary line — blocks lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves T2–T9; covers the lateral chest wall where rib fractures are most common
Rib fracture complications: inadequate analgesia leads to splinting, reduced respiratory effort, retained secretions, and pneumonia — especially dangerous in the elderly and those with ≥3 fractures
Elderly rib fractures: mortality increases ~19% per additional rib fracture; flail chest (3+ consecutive ribs fractured in ≥2 places) = paradoxical breathing → NIV or intubation
Multimodal analgesia: regular paracetamol 1 g QDS + regular NSAID (if not contraindicated) + thoracic regional block + PRN opioid — avoid opioid monotherapy
Incentive spirometry and respiratory physiotherapy: mandatory post-rib fractures — deep breathing, coughing technique, early mobilisation; reduces pneumonia from 10% to ~3% in RCTs
CT chest for all significant rib fractures: detects pneumothorax (30% missed on erect CXR), haemothorax, pulmonary contusion, aortic injury — never rely solely on CXR in high-mechanism trauma

deep_dive.heading: SAPB Technique at the Bedside
steps: Position: lateral decubitus or sitting; POCUS high-frequency linear probe in coronal plane at 4th–6th rib level midaxillary line
Identify: ribs → intercostal muscles → serratus anterior muscle (superficial to ribs, diagonal fibres), latissimus dorsi (more superficial)
In-plane needle approach: insert anterior to posterior, advance to deep surface of serratus anterior muscle
Confirm correct plane: inject 1–2 mL LA and observe spread between serratus and intercostal muscle (hydrodissection)
Volume: 20–30 mL levobupivacaine 0.25% or bupivacaine 0.25% total — covers multiple dermatomes
Onset 15–30 min; duration 6–12h; catheter can be placed for continuous infusion in severe cases

quiz.question: A 72-year-old has 4 rib fractures (6th–9th left) after a fall. Pain 8/10 on inspiration, SpO2 93% on 4L O2. What is the optimal analgesia strategy?
options: IV morphine PCA alone — fastest onset
Oral codeine plus paracetamol — standard combination
Multimodal: paracetamol + NSAID + SAPB ultrasound-guided + PRN opioid + respiratory physiotherapy
Reassure and discharge — CXR shows no pneumothorax
quiz.explanation: 4 rib fractures in an elderly patient with SpO2 93% is a serious injury. Multimodal analgesia including SAPB is evidence-based (PMID 42159402). Opioid monotherapy increases sedation and respiratory depression — the opposite of what is needed. CT chest is required to exclude occult injuries.

source.title: Serratus Anterior Plane Block for Acute Rib Fractures in the Emergency Department

modules.title: Paediatric Asthma in the ED — One Dose of Dexamethasone Is Probably Enough

bullets.text: Dexamethasone 0.15–0.6 mg/kg PO (max 10 mg) is the preferred oral corticosteroid for paediatric asthma — better palatability than prednisolone, fewer vomiting episodes

Single vs two doses (Ann Emerg Med 2026, PMID 41575401): nearly two-thirds of children received 2 doses; two doses NOT associated with improved outcomes — a single dose of dexamethasone may be sufficient for most children
Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg (weight-based) nebulised every 20 min for first hour in moderate-severe attack; MDI + spacer is equivalent or superior to nebulised in mild-moderate attacks
Ipratropium bromide 250 mcg (up to 500 mcg in >12 years) with first 3 salbutamol nebulisers — reduces admission rate in moderate-severe attacks (NNT ~8)
IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 min: use in severe/life-threatening attacks or no response to initial nebulisers — reduces admission rate (NNT 5–6)
Life-threatening features: SpO2 <92% on O2, silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness, cyanosis — call anaesthetics immediately; never sedate without intubation equipment ready
Azithromycin for preschool wheeze (NEJM 2026, PMID 42149992): NO benefit over placebo for acute wheezing in preschoolers — do not prescribe macrolides for viral wheeze

deep_dive.heading: Severity Scoring and Step-Up Treatment
steps: Mild: SpO2 ≥95%, mild wheeze, talking in sentences — salbutamol MDI/spacer × 4 puffs, oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose
Moderate: SpO2 92–95%, moderate wheeze, sentences interrupted — salbutamol + ipratropium nebulised × 3 over 60 min, dexamethasone, IV access
Severe: SpO2 <92%, severe wheeze, words only — back-to-back nebs + ipratropium, IV MgSO4 40 mg/kg, continuous monitoring, anaesthetic review
Life-threatening: silent chest, exhaustion, altered consciousness — immediate anaesthetic/ITU, consider heliox, prepare for intubation
Discharge criteria: SpO2 ≥95% on room air for ≥1h, no wheeze, tolerating oral fluids, education — spacer + written action plan

quiz.question: A 7-year-old with moderate asthma has received three salbutamol nebulisers and ipratropium. SpO2 93% on 4L O2. Which is the next most appropriate intervention?
options: Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally — possible bacterial trigger
IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg over 20 minutes
Increase salbutamol to 10 mg nebulised every 5 minutes
Discharge with oral prednisolone and GP follow-up
quiz.explanation: SpO2 93% after 3 nebulisers = severe asthma. IV magnesium sulphate is the next step — evidence shows it reduces hospital admission and improves bronchodilation in the ED. Azithromycin has no role in acute viral wheeze (NEJM 2026). Discharge at SpO2 93% is unsafe.

source.title: Dexamethasone Treatment Regimen and Clinical Outcomes in Children With Asthma Exacerbations

modules.title: ED Boarding — Early Clinical Deterioration and the Safety Evidence You Need

bullets.text: ED boarding: Ann Emerg Med 2026 (PMID 41860510) — boarding duration independently associated with increased odds of early clinical deterioration (ECD); ECD occurs in 2–5% of boarded patients
ECD definition: unplanned escalation to ICU, cardiac arrest, or death within 24h of ED admission — risk increases with each additional hour of boarding

BMJ 2026 (PMID 42521355): a patient died from sepsis after ED discharge due to overcrowding — NHS England serious incident; overcrowding directly causing missed deterioration is now a medico-legal standard
Monitoring standards for boarded patients: NEWS2 documented at least every 2 hours; medical review with every 3-point NEWS2 change; document when suboptimal monitoring is capacity-imposed
Systemic risk factors: boarded corridor patients have higher rates of missed vital signs, delayed treatment, and medication errors — document when monitoring is constrained by operational pressures
RCEM guidance: patient safety must not be compromised by operational pressures — if a patient cannot be monitored safely, escalate to senior clinician and document in notes
Professional duty: document boarding time, monitoring challenges, and escalation requests — creates the evidence base for system change AND provides medico-legal protection

deep_dive.heading: NEWS2 Thresholds and Escalation in the Boarded Patient
points: NEWS2 ≥5: 4-hourly minimum monitoring; escalate to senior clinician; request urgent clinical review
NEWS2 ≥7: continuous monitoring; emergency senior review within 30 min; consider HDU/ICU without waiting for bed
Corridor patients: document that monitoring frequency is constrained by environment — this triggers an incident report
Escalation pathway: charge nurse → site manager → on-call consultant → medical director — use the full chain, document each step
CQC and NHSE: repeated sub-standard monitoring of boarded patients is a regulatory risk for the department

quiz.question: A 68-year-old admitted patient has been in the ED corridor for 6 hours. NEWS2 rises from 4 to 7. No monitored bays are available. What is the correct action?
options: Check observations every 4 hours — NEWS2 4 protocol
Document NEWS2 7, escalate to senior clinician for emergency review, document monitoring limitations, consider direct ICU/HDU referral
Discharge and readmit when a monitored space becomes available
Call for a ward review when a doctor is free
quiz.explanation: NEWS2 7 requires emergency senior review within 30 minutes. Monitoring limitations imposed by overcrowding must be documented as a patient safety incident. Direct ICU/HDU escalation should not wait for a medical ward bed. This is both a patient safety issue and a professional documentation requirement.

source.title: Early Clinical Deterioration Among Emergency Department Boarders

modules.title: Paediatric Drowning — Rescue Breathing Is Mandatory, Not Optional

bullets.text: Resuscitation 2026 nationwide study (PMID 41819340): in paediatric drowning OHCA, compression-only CPR (CO-CPR) was associated with WORSE survival and neurological outcomes than standard CPR with rescue breaths

Mechanism: drowning is an asphyxial arrest — primary hypoxia precedes circulatory collapse; oxygen delivery through rescue breathing is essential, unlike adult VF arrest where compressions alone are effective
Paediatric CPR ratios: 2-rescuer 15:2 (compressions:breaths); 1-rescuer 30:2 — rescue breaths are integral, not optional adjuncts
Bystander rescue breathing in drowning: RCUK strongly advocates CPR with rescue breaths for drowning; compression-only bystander CPR is an inadequate response in asphyxial arrest
ED management of near-drowning: RSI early if GCS ≤8 or respiratory failure; lung protective ventilation 6 mL/kg IBW; PEEP 5–8 cmH2O; CXR + ABG + blood glucose; active rewarming if <35°C
Hypothermic drowning: not dead until warm and dead — resuscitate until core temperature ≥32°C before declaring death; ECMO-assisted rewarming for severe hypothermia at ECMO-capable centres
Public CPR teaching: all public CPR training must include rescue breaths for children and drowning victims — CO-CPR guidance for adult VF arrest does NOT apply to paediatric drowning

deep_dive.heading: Paediatric Drowning — ED Resuscitation Protocol
steps: Airway: immediate RSI if GCS ≤8, apnoeic, or SpO2 <90% despite high-flow O2
Breathing: lung protective ventilation; suction airway if contaminated; consider surfactant in infants
Circulation: IV/IO access; 10 mL/kg balanced crystalloid if haemodynamically compromised; check blood glucose (hypoglycaemia is common)
Temperature: rectal or oesophageal temperature; active rewarming if <35°C; ECMO referral if <32°C with no ROSC
Neurology: post-ROSC care; prevent hyperthermia; target glucose 4–8 mmol/L; seizure watch; CT head if traumatic mechanism
Withdrawal of care: do NOT terminate resuscitation while hypothermic — transfer to ECMO centre if no ROSC and temperature <28°C

quiz.question: A bystander pulls a 6-year-old from a swimming pool. The child is unresponsive and not breathing. What type of CPR should the bystander perform?
options: Compression-only CPR — as per standard public bystander guidance
Standard CPR with rescue breaths (30:2 if alone, 15:2 if two rescuers) — rescue breathing is essential in drowning
Rescue breaths only — no chest compressions until the ambulance arrives
Wait for EMS with AED — bystander CPR may cause harm in a child
quiz.explanation: Drowning is an asphyxial arrest — rescue breaths are mandatory. Compression-only CPR is significantly inferior in paediatric drowning (Resuscitation 2026, PMID 41819340). CO-CPR guidance was designed for witnessed adult VF arrest, not paediatric asphyxial arrest. Every second without oxygenation worsens outcome.

source.title: Decline in rescue breathing and its impact on outcomes in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to drowning
